docs.title: Beyond the Honeymoon: OTel in Practice
docs.text: Welcome to the Perform hands-on training. The Vegas Casino application you are running today ships with deliberately broken observability. In three hours you take it from broken traces to a production-grade OpenTelemetry pipeline — SDK first, collector second — and watch every fix land in Dynatrace.

docs.title: The honeymoon problem
docs.text:
Every OpenTelemetry rollout follows the same curve. The honeymoon: a quickstart gets traces flowing, dashboards light up, everyone is happy. Then reality arrives — a service drops off the trace, a metric dimension explodes into millions of series, an email address shows up in a log — and nobody knows which config surface fixes it, because the config was never really owned. It was copied.

Today you take ownership. The casino has real defects, planted on purpose. You diagnose them in Dynatrace, fix them in configuration — never in application code — and verify each fix in the tenant.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text: Hour Module You will… 0:00–0:15 M0 — Environment setup Codespace up, kind cluster healthy, Dynatrace connected, casino deployed 0:15–0:45 M1 — Tour the broken casino Diagnose the trace-context defect; fix W3C propagation 0:45–1:15 M2 — SDK configuration by file Move the Java service to declarative otel-config.yaml 1:25–2:05 M3 — The collector as control point Fix high-cardinality metrics and PII logs at the source and the collector 2:05–2:35 M4 — Sampling strategy Cut ingest cost with tail sampling; keep RED metrics with spanmetrics 2:35–2:55 M5 — Operating at scale Leave with the enterprise readiness checklist

docs.title: The environment
docs.text:
Everything runs in your GitHub Codespace — nothing is installed on your laptop but a browser:

flowchart LR k6["k6 load-gen"] -->|HTTP| fe["frontend"] fe -->|gRPC| games["slots / roulette / dice / blackjack"] fe -->|HTTP| scoring["scoring (Java)"] fe -->|gRPC| dash["dashboard"] dash -->|HTTP| scoring games --> redis[("redis")] scoring --> pg[("postgresql")] fe -. "OTLP/gRPC" .-> gw games -. "OTLP/gRPC" .-> gw scoring -. "OTLP/gRPC" .-> gw dash -. "OTLP/gRPC" .-> gw gw["otel-gateway-collector.observability:4317k8sattributes → cumulativetodelta → batch"] --> dt[("Dynatrace tenant")]
  • kind cluster in your Codespace, one per attendee
  • Vegas Casino — Node.js, Python, Go and Java microservices (namespace casino)
  • OTel collectors — a DaemonSet for node logs and a gateway collector that enriches and exports to Dynatrace (namespace observability)
  • Dynatrace — shared tenant; your cluster is identified by your unique K8S_CLUSTER_NAME
  • GitOps — an in-cluster Git host (Gitea) and Argo CD sync the casino namespace. You fix defects by editing a manifest and committing — the same loop you would use in production

docs.title: How to use this guide
docs.text:
• Command blocks are meant to be pasted into the Codespace terminal.
  • Dynatrace check sections tell you exactly what to look for in the tenant. A fix that does not show up in Dynatrace did not happen.
  • Each module ends with a Definition of done. A helper will check you off before you move on.
  • Solutions for each defect hunt are collapsed — try the hunt first, then click to reveal.

Start here: open M0 — Environment Setup.

docs.title: M1 — Tour the broken casino: OTel core principles
docs.text: Goal: play the casino, read its telemetry, and correctly diagnose the first planted defect — traces that break at the slots service. You fix it with one line of configuration. 30 minutes.

docs.title: Concepts (5 min)
docs.text:
Three ideas carry this module:

  1. Signals. Traces, metrics, logs — three independent pipelines out of the SDK. A service can emit one perfectly and lose the other two; you will see exactly that today.
  2. Context propagation. A trace crosses a process boundary only if both sides agree on the wire format. The W3C standard is the traceparent header. If the caller injects traceparent but the callee only knows a proprietary header, the callee starts a new, disconnected trace. The trace did not "fail" — it was never one trace to begin with.
  3. Resource = identity. service.name, service.version, service.namespace describe who emits the telemetry. Dashboards, owners, and alerts key off these. Wrong identity means operationally invisible.

And the split of responsibility: instrumentation lives in the SDK; the collector only receives what the SDK sends. If the SDK mis-propagates or mislabels, no collector can fix it downstream. That is why this training fixes SDK problems first (M1–M2) and collector problems second (M3–M4).

docs.title: The defect hunt
docs.text: Keep the frontend port-forward running (M0), make sure you played at least a few rounds of slots and one other game, then open Dynatrace.

docs.title: Hunt — the trace that was never whole
docs.text:
1. Open Distributed traces, filter to your k8s.cluster.name, last 30 minutes.
  2. Search for traces containing the service vegas-slots-service.

What you should see: every trace that reaches slots is short. Look at one: it contains slots_spin (or an equivalent slots server span) as the root span — no caller above it. Compare with a roulette or blackjack round: those traces start at vegas-frontend-service and flow down through the game service in one connected flame graph.

So slots is not "losing" spans. Slots was never in your trace: each request became its own orphan trace, because the context arriving from the frontend was ignored.

Why is the context ignored? (click after the hunt)

The frontend injects W3C tracecontext — the standard. The slots service is configured to only understand a proprietary single-header format from the 2021 in-house framework (x-vegas-trace). The two sides never agree, so slots starts a fresh trace for every request.

Open the evidence in the repo — in services/common/propagators.js there is a VegasLegacyPropagator, and the slots deployment selects it with:

- name: OTEL_PROPAGATORS
  value: "vegas-legacy"

Every other service uses the default (tracecontext,baggage), which is why they stay connected.

docs.title: The fix
docs.text:
Configuration lives in Git, not in the running cluster. Fix it where the manifest lives:

  1. Open Gitea (http://localhost:30001), repo casino/casino.

  2. Open 30-slots.yaml and find the env block of the slots container:

    # Slots still correlates via the legacy in-house header from the 2021
# framework instead of W3C Trace Context
- name: OTEL_PROPAGATORS
  value: "vegas-legacy"

  3. Change the value to the W3C propagators:

    - name: OTEL_PROPAGATORS
  value: "tracecontext,baggage"

  4. Commit the change (Gitea web editor: pencil icon → edit → commit).

Argo CD picks up the commit and rolls the slots deployment. Watch it:

kubectl -n casino rollout status deploy/vegas-casino-slots

docs.title: Dynatrace check
docs.text:
1. Play a few slots rounds (or wait ~1 minute for the k6 load generator).
  2. Distributed traces → filter k8s.cluster.name = yours, service vegas-slots-service, last 5 minutes.

What you should see: traces now start at vegas-frontend-service and flow frontend → slots in one connected flame graph. The orphan-rooted slots traces stop appearing (give it a couple of minutes for old traces to age out of the view).

Extra evidence: open any connected trace and inspect the span attributes on the slots span — no proprietary header, clean W3C parentage.

Why this matters more than it looks

Orphan traces quietly destroy the promise of distributed tracing: response time attribution, failure blast-radius, service-flow topology — all keyed on connected traces. And nothing "errored": every span was exported, both before and after the fix. The only signal was shape, which you had to go look for.

docs.title: Definition of done — M1
docs.text:
• You found orphan-rooted slots traces in Dynatrace and explained the mechanism (inject/extract format mismatch)
  • You can name the config surface that fixes it (OTEL_PROPAGATORS on the SDK, owned by the workload's manifest)
  • You fixed it via a Git commit, not a kubectl patch
  • Connected frontend → slots traces now visible in Dynatrace

Next: M2 — SDK configuration by file.

docs.title: M2 — SDK configuration by file: declarative config
docs.text: Goal: take the Java Scoring Service from code-first SDK configuration to a declarative otel-config.yaml, injected with zero code changes. 30 minutes.

docs.title: Concepts (5 min)
docs.text:
There are three ways to configure an SDK, in increasing order of scale:

  1. Env vars — OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_PROPAGATORS, … Fine for a handful of settings; becomes env-var soup at fleet scale.
  2. Code — an OpenTelemetryConfig class building the SDK by hand. Maximum control, but every configuration change is a rebuild and redeploy of the application.
  3. Declarative file — one otel-config.yaml, version-controlled, reviewed, and mounted into the workload. The schema is shared across languages; today the Java zero-code agent implements it via OTEL_CONFIG_FILE.

The one rule everyone gets bitten by

When the SDK reads a config file, environment variables are ignored unless the file references them with ${ENV_VAR}. This is the single most common "why is my config ignored?" question in the lab.

docs.title: The problem: config welded into code
docs.text:
The Scoring Service (Java, Spring Boot) configures OTel in code — services/scoring/.../config/OpenTelemetryConfig.java builds its own tracer provider with a hard-coded OTLP exporter. Consequences you can observe right now in Dynatrace:

  • Traces from vegas-scoring-service flow (the code exports them).
  • No JVM metrics — the code never wires a meter provider.
  • No logs — the code never wires a logger provider. Java logs go to stdout, unstructured, invisible to OTLP.

Want to change the sampler? Rebuild the jar. Want logs? Write Java. This is the anti-pattern the declarative file replaces.

docs.title: The lab: zero-code instrumentation via the operator
docs.text: Your cluster runs the OpenTelemetry Operator (namespace observability). It can inject the Java agent into any workload — no Dockerfile change, no code.

docs.title: Step 1 — create the config and the Instrumentation CR
docs.text:
In Gitea, repo casino/casino, create a new file 21-scoring-otel.yaml (Add file → New file) with:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: scoring-otel-config
data:
  otel-config.yaml: |
    file_format: "1.1"

    resource:
      attributes:
        - name: service.name
          value: vegas-scoring-service
        - name: service.namespace
          value: vegas-casino
      detectors:            # fill in host/process/container identity
        - host:
        - process:
        - container:

    propagator:
      composite:
        - tracecontext:
        - baggage:

    tracer_provider:
      sampler:
        parent_based:
          root:
            always_on: {}          # M4 revisits this
      processors:
        - batch:
            exporter:
              otlp:
                endpoint: http://otel-gateway-collector.observability.svc.cluster.local:4317
                tls:
                  insecure: true

    meter_provider:
      readers:
        - periodic:
            exporter:
              otlp:
                endpoint: http://otel-gateway-collector.observability.svc.cluster.local:4317
                tls:
                  insecure: true

    logger_provider:
      processors:
        - batch:
            exporter:
              otlp:
                endpoint: http://otel-gateway-collector.observability.svc.cluster.local:4317
                tls:
                  insecure: true
---
apiVersion: opentelemetry.io/v1alpha1
kind: Instrumentation
metadata:
  name: casino-java
spec:
  java:
    env:
      - name: OTEL_CONFIG_FILE
        value: /etc/otel/otel-config.yaml

Read it before you commit — every block maps to a concept from M1: resource identity, propagation, per-signal pipelines (tracer / meter / logger providers), each with its own batch processor and OTLP exporter.

Note what the file does not contain: any of the OTEL_* env vars from the deployment. If we needed one, it would have to appear as ${VAR} inside the file to be honored at all.

Commit the file.

docs.title: Step 2 — wire the scoring deployment to the agent and the file
docs.text:
Edit 20-scoring.yaml in the same repo. Three changes:

  1. Add the injection annotation to the pod template metadata (the template.metadata.annotations block — create it if missing):

    instrumentation.opentelemetry.io/inject-java: "casino-java"

  2. Add the env var pointing at the mounted file, in the container env block:

    - name: OTEL_CONFIG_FILE
  value: /etc/otel/otel-config.yaml

  3. Mount the ConfigMap — add to the container volumeMounts and the pod volumes:

    # container:
volumeMounts:
  - name: scoring-otel-config
    mountPath: /etc/otel
    readOnly: true
# pod spec:
volumes:
  - name: scoring-otel-config
    configMap:
      name: scoring-otel-config

Commit. Argo CD syncs; watch the rollout:

kubectl -n casino rollout status deploy/vegas-casino-scoring
kubectl -n casino get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=vegas-casino -o name | grep scoring

Not rolling?

Argo CD only syncs files it can render. YAML-indentation errors in the ConfigMap (the | block) are the usual suspect — check the Argo CD app status at http://localhost:30002 before you debug anything else.

docs.title: Step 3 — verify in Dynatrace
docs.text:
Give it a minute, then with your cluster filter:

  1. Metrics — search metric names for jvm_ or open the scoring service's infrastructure view: JVM runtime metrics appear for vegas-scoring-service — they were absent before, because the meter provider only exists now, in the file.
  2. Logs — open Logs, filter service.name = vegas-scoring-service: structured logback lines now arrive, each correlated with a trace.
  3. Traces — still flowing frontend → game → scoring, as in M1.
Known wrinkle — you may see double export

The application still contains its legacy programmatic config (OpenTelemetryConfig.java), which keeps exporting its own manual spans. If a trace shows near-duplicate scoring spans, that is the old code path, not your file config. In production you would delete the programmatic config and let the file be the single source of truth; for the lab it is harmless — the new signals (JVM metrics, logs) come only from the file.

docs.title: Definition of done — M2
docs.text:
• You can explain the three config surfaces and when each wins
  • You can state the env-var rule for file mode without looking it up
  • 21-scoring-otel.yaml committed: ConfigMap + Instrumentation CR
  • JVM metrics and logs from vegas-scoring-service visible in Dynatrace
  • Traces still connected end-to-end

Next: M3 — The collector as control point.

docs.title: M3 — The collector as control point
docs.text: Goal: learn the collector pipeline, then fix two more planted defects — a high-cardinality metric and PII in logs — at the SDK and defend them at the collector. 40 minutes. This is the centerpiece module.

docs.title: Concepts (5 min)
docs.text:
A collector pipeline is receivers → processors → exporters, per signal (traces / metrics / logs). The canonical processor order:

memory_limiter → enrichment → filtering/transform → (aggregation) → batch → exporters

Why this order, one sentence each:

  • memory_limiter first — shed load before spending memory on it.
  • Enrichment before filtering — you cannot filter on an attribute you have not added yet.
  • batch last — batch once, after all mutation, right before export.

And the thesis of this module: the collector is a control point. It sits between every workload and the backend, so it is the one place you can enforce policy — cardinality limits, PII scrubbing, routing, sampling — even when an individual SDK misbehaves. But the control point only sees what reaches it: the cheapest fixes are still at the source, which is why every defect below gets fixed twice — at the SDK, then backstopped at the collector.

docs.title: Tour — your collector, the reference pipeline
docs.text:
The gateway collector runs as an OpenTelemetryCollector CR in your repo. Open it in your Codespace editor:

code observability/collectors/gateway.yaml   # or just open the file

Find the config: block and read the pipelines. This one is the reference answer for processor order:

  • memory_limiter first, on every pipeline
  • k8sattributes — enrichment: attaches k8s.pod.name, k8s.namespace.name, and friends (it can do this because the DaemonSet forwards pod metadata and the gateway runs in-cluster)
  • cumulativetodelta — metrics pipeline only: counters arrive cumulative, Dynatrace wants rates
  • batch last, then otlphttp export to your Dynatrace tenant

You will edit this file in the exercises. The discipline around it is config-as-product: edit in Git → validate offline → apply → verify. Never kubectl edit a live collector.

docs.title: Exercise A — the metric that ate the tenant (high cardinality)
Find it
docs.text:
The k6 load generator plays constantly with generated usernames (k6user_<timestamp>_<random>). Look at what that does to one metric.

In Dynatrace, open Metrics and search for casino.bet.amount. This is a histogram — amount wagered per game round, USD — recorded by the frontend with a game dimension. Sensible.

Now inspect its dimensions: filter or split by player_id.

What you should see: player_id exists and has a value per player — and every k6 round mints a new player. A histogram's series count is dimensions × buckets: unbounded player_id means unbounded time series. Run the load for an hour and this one metric generates more series than the rest of the casino combined. Cardinality is the tax you pay before you see any bill — it degrades queries and dashboards first, ingest cost second.

Where does player_id come from? (click after the hunt)

The frontend deployment asks for it — a "per-player breakdown requested by analytics" — via an env var in 50-frontend.yaml:

# Per-player metric breakdown requested by the analytics team
- name: CASINO_PLAYER_LEVEL_METRICS
  value: "true"

With it, services/common/casino-metrics.js adds attributes.player_id = username to every bet recording. The ask was reasonable; the dimension key was unbounded.

docs.title: Fix it at the source (SDK)
docs.text:
In Gitea, repo casino/casino, edit 50-frontend.yaml:

- name: CASINO_PLAYER_LEVEL_METRICS
  value: "false"

Commit, and watch Argo CD roll the frontend:

kubectl -n casino rollout status deploy/vegas-casino-frontend

docs.title: Backstop it at the collector (control point)
docs.text:
The SDK fix only holds while every deployment keeps that knob false. A control point makes the policy structural: the gateway drops the dimension no matter what workloads send.

In your Codespace repo, edit observability/collectors/gateway.yaml. In the config: block, add a transform processor:

    processors:
      transform/drop_player_id:
        error_mode: ignore
        metric_statements:
          - context: datapoint
            statements:
              - delete_key(attributes, "player_id")

And reference it in the metrics pipeline, after enrichment and before batch:

    service:
      pipelines:
        metrics:
          receivers: [otlp]
          processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, transform/drop_player_id, cumulativetodelta, batch]
          exporters: [otlphttp/dynatrace]

(Keep the processor list already present in your file; the point is where the new one sits.)

Apply the config-as-product discipline:

bash observability/validate.sh
kubectl apply -f observability/collectors/gateway.yaml
kubectl -n observability rollout status deploy/otel-gateway-collector

docs.title: Dynatrace check
docs.text:
1. Play a few rounds (or wait for k6), then re-check casino.bet.amount: new datapoints no longer carry player_id; existing split-by-player results stop gaining new series.
  2. The game dimension survives — you lost nothing you actually chart.

docs.title: Exercise B — the email in the log (PII)
Find it
docs.text:
Register/login as your player at http://localhost:3000 — the UI you used in M0 — then in Dynatrace open Logs and filter service.name = vegas-frontend-service, search for login_audit.

What you should see: a structured log entry per login, containing — in plain text — the player's email address, client IP, and user agent. Player-tracking data in a shared observability backend is a compliance problem (GDPR and friends), and a trust problem: everyone with tenant log access just became a data handler.

Where does it come from? (click after the hunt)

Another "request from a team" — compliance sign-off wanted verbose audit logging — wired as an env var in 50-frontend.yaml:

# Verbose audit logging for compliance sign-off
- name: AUDIT_LOG_VERBOSITY
  value: "verbose"

In verbose mode the frontend's login_audit logs raw values. The app ships redaction helpers (services/common/pii.js: masked email, hashed IP, masked username) that are used automatically in every other mode.

docs.title: Fix it at the source (SDK)
docs.text:
In Gitea, edit 50-frontend.yaml:

- name: AUDIT_LOG_VERBOSITY
  value: "redacted"

Commit, let Argo CD roll the frontend, then log in again and re-check the login_audit entries.

What you should see: emails masked (j****@…), IPs hashed to a short hex digest, usernames partially masked. The audit event survives — you kept the audit trail and dropped the liability.

docs.title: Backstop it at the collector (stretch)
docs.text: Same pattern as Exercise A, now for logs. A transform on the logs pipeline can scrub attributes or body fields even if a workload ships raw values — with one caveat: body fields are strings, so a collector-side regex scrub of the body is possible but brittle; attribute-level scrubbing is robust. When you run collectors as the enforcement point at fleet scale, this backstop is what makes PII policy enforceable in one place. If you have time, try an attributes/delete_key action for user.email in the logs pipeline using the same steps as Exercise A.

docs.title: The fleet-scale version of what you just did
docs.text: You enforced policy by editing Git, validating, applying — the honest, small-fleet workflow. At dozens of clusters and hundreds of collectors, that workflow gets a product around it: OpAMP (the remote-management protocol for OTel collectors) and managed-configuration platforms such as BindPlane — configuration as a versioned artifact, validated, rolled out staged (canary first), with history and one-click rollback, instead of N repos to herd. Same discipline you practiced here; the tooling scales it.

docs.title: Definition of done — M3
docs.text:
• You can recite the canonical processor order and defend each position
  • You found player_id on casino.bet.amount and explained why unbounded dimensions are dangerous
  • Source fix committed (CASINO_PLAYER_LEVEL_METRICS=false) and verified
  • Collector backstop for player_id validated and applied
  • You found raw PII in login_audit logs, fixed the verbosity knob, and verified redaction in Dynatrace
  • You can say, in one sentence, why the collector is the right place for a policy backstop — and why the source fix still comes first

Next: M4 — Sampling: cost/fidelity strategy.

docs.title: M4 — Sampling: cost/fidelity strategy
docs.text: Goal: cut ingest cost without losing the traces you would actually debug. Break it naively first, then build a defensible policy on the collector. 30 minutes.

docs.title: Concepts (5 min)
docs.text:
Two places to sample, two trade-offs:

  • Head sampling — decided at span creation, in the SDK (parent_based + traceidratio). Nearly free, but blind: the decision is made before you know whether the request fails or drags.
  • Tail sampling — decided when the trace completes, in the collector (tail_sampling processor). Informed: it has seen the errors and the durations. Expensive: the collector buffers every trace until decision time.

The pattern that survives contact with production: head sampling generous (usually always_on in-cluster), tail sampling smart at the aggregation tier — keep all errors, keep all slow traces, sample the rest — plus the spanmetrics connector computing RED metrics (rate / errors / duration) from every span before sampling drops anything, so your dashboards survive aggressive sampling.

docs.title: Step 1 — baseline: measure before you touch anything
docs.text:
The k6 load generator drives continuous traffic. In Dynatrace, Distributed traces, your cluster filter, last 15 minutes. Record:

  • trace count: ______
  • traces with status = ERROR (add the filter): ______
  • rough p95 of a game-service endpoint (e.g. from the response-time distribution): ______

This is the fidelity baseline. Every change below is judged against it.

docs.title: Step 2 — break it: naive head sampling
docs.text:
If you sampled 10% at the head you would save ~90% of span ingest. Try it on one service. In Gitea, 33-blackjack.yaml, add to the container env:

- name: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER
  value: "parentbased_traceidratio"
- name: OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG
  value: "0.1"

Commit, wait for the rollout, give it 5 minutes of traffic.

What you should see in Dynatrace: blackjack spans drop to roughly 10%. Now filter your view to status = ERROR: errors dropped to ~10% too. You saved money and lost ~90% of your visibility into the exact requests you would be paged for. Keep that feeling — it is the entire argument for tail sampling.

Revert it now (delete the two env vars, commit) so blackjack is honest again for the rest of the lab.

docs.title: Step 3 — build it: tail sampling on the gateway
docs.text: Sampling policy belongs at the aggregation tier where the whole trace is visible. In your Codespace repo, edit observability/collectors/gateway.yaml.

docs.title: 3a. Drop health checks before buffering
docs.text:
No reason to buffer spans you will never keep. Add a filter processor:

    processors:
      filter/noise:
        traces:
          span:
            - 'attributes["http.route"] == "/health" or attributes["http.route"] == "/healthz"'

And put it in the traces pipeline right after k8sattributes.

docs.title: 3b. Add the tail sampling policy
docs.text:
processors:
      tail_sampling:
        decision_wait: 10s
        num_traces: 50000
        policies:
          - name: keep-errors
            type: status_code
            status_code:
              status_codes: [ERROR]
          - name: keep-slow
            type: latency
            latency:
              threshold_ms: 500
          - name: baseline
            type: probabilistic
            probabilistic:
              sampling_percentage: 10

Read it as three sentences: every failed trace is kept; every trace slower than 500 ms is kept; everything else survives at 10%. Those numbers are the cost/fidelity dial you will defend to your platform budget holder.

docs.title: 3c. Add the spanmetrics connector
docs.text:
Sampling will delete most traces; RED metrics should not follow them down. Add a connector section (top level of config:, next to processors:):

    connectors:
      spanmetrics:
        histogram:
          explicit:
            buckets: [5ms, 10ms, 25ms, 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2.5s, 5s, 10s]
        dimensions:
          - name: http.method
          - name: http.route
        exemplars:
          enabled: true

Wire both sides — traces export into it, metrics read from it:

    service:
      pipelines:
        traces:
          receivers: [otlp]
          processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, filter/noise, tail_sampling, batch]
          exporters: [otlphttp/dynatrace, spanmetrics]
        metrics:
          receivers: [otlp, spanmetrics]
          processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, transform/drop_player_id, cumulativetodelta, batch]
          exporters: [otlphttp/dynatrace]

(If you skipped the M3 stretch, your metrics processors simply will not have transform/drop_player_id. Keep the rest of your own file's lists.)

docs.title: 3d. Validate, apply, verify
docs.text:
bash observability/validate.sh
kubectl apply -f observability/collectors/gateway.yaml
kubectl -n observability rollout status deploy/otel-gateway-collector
kubectl -n observability logs deploy/otel-gateway-collector --tail=20

No restart loops, no config-rejected lines in the log — then give it 5 minutes and re-measure in Dynatrace (same window as the baseline):

  • trace count (target: roughly 10–20% of baseline): ______
  • ERROR traces (target: ~unchanged from baseline): ______
  • spanmetrics present: search metrics for traces.span.metrics.calls — RED series per http.route of the game services: yes/no

What you should see: ingest way down; every error trace still there; RED metric charts that keep showing the full traffic shape — even though most of the corresponding traces no longer exist.

If errors go missing

decision_wait: 10s is shorter than some multi-service traces take to complete — spans arriving after the decision miss the vote. Raise it to 15s. And watch collector memory: num_traces buffers decisions; on a small kind node, 50000 is plenty, at fleet scale it is a tuning knob.

docs.title: Definition of done — M4
docs.text:
• Baseline, naive-head, and tail-sampling measurements recorded
  • You can state your policy in one sentence ("all errors, all >500 ms, 10% of the rest") and defend both what it saves (ingest) and what it costs (decision latency, collector memory, blind spots under threshold)
  • spanmetrics RED series visible for game services
  • ERROR visibility ~unchanged vs baseline while total traces dropped

Next: M5 — Operating at scale.

docs.title: M5 — Operating at scale + the readiness checklist
docs.text: Goal: compress what you just did into an operating model you can take home. 20 minutes, talk + demo.

docs.title: What you actually did today
docs.text:
Module Defect Fix surface Verified by M1 Trace-context break (x-vegas-trace vs W3C) SDK propagators (OTEL_PROPAGATORS) Connected flame graph M2 Config welded into code Declarative otel-config.yaml + zero-code agent JVM metrics + logs appear M3 High-cardinality metric (player_id) SDK knob + collector transform Series growth stops M3 PII in logs (raw email/IP) SDK verbosity knob (+ collector backstop) Redacted login_audit M4 Cost/fidelity of ingest tail_sampling + spanmetrics on the gateway Errors kept at ~15% volume

One pattern under all five: the defect was never in the application logic — it was in configuration nobody owned. Observability went production-grade the moment configuration became a reviewed artifact in Git.

docs.title: The enterprise readiness checklist
docs.text: The checklist below is the take-home from Beyond the Honeymoon: OTel at Enterprise Scale. Every item maps to something you touched today.

docs.title: Configuration safety
docs.text:
• One file, in Git, per workload — declarative SDK config (otel-config.yaml), not env-var soup, not code (M2).
  • Validate before apply — offline validation is the gate (bash observability/validate.sh → otelcol validate under the hood). You saw why: a config that looks right can crash-loop a live collector while validation passes on the wrong assumption.
  • Pin versions — collector, operator, SDKs: observability/versions.env exists so upgrades are a deliberate act, not an accident (the casino's dependency baseline was itself a pinned, verified upgrade).
  • Literal bools and escaped env — collector config gotchas that pass validation and fail at runtime; the gateway CR in this repo documents two of them in comments. Read your collector's comments; write yours.

docs.title: Pipeline hygiene
docs.text:
• Canonical processor order — memory_limiter first, batch last, enrichment before filtering (M3).
  • Cardinality budget — every metric dimension is a decision; unbounded dimensions are rejected at design time or dropped at the control point (M3).
  • PII policy at a control point — source-side redaction first, collector-side enforcement as the backstop (M3).
  • Sampling as an explicit policy — keep-errors / keep-slow / probabilistic-baseline, with spanmetrics so RED survives (M4).

docs.title: Fleet operations
docs.text:
• Staged rollouts — canary collector first, then the fleet; history and one-click rollback. You practiced the manual discipline (validate → apply → verify); at fleet scale this becomes OpAMP-based management (e.g. BindPlane) — same discipline, productized.
  • Persistent queues + backpressure — the gateway exporter ships with sending_queue and retry_on_failure; size them for your backend's worst bad day, and let memory_limiter shed before the OOM does.
  • Propagate, always — W3C tracecontext everywhere; proprietary formats only as an explicit, documented exception (M1).

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• The OTel spec for declarative SDK configuration — the file format from M2, heading toward every language.
  • Collector blueprints — don't start from blank YAML; start from a reviewed reference (this repo's gateway CR is one).
  • The book: Beyond the Honeymoon: OTel at Enterprise Scale — the full lifecycle of a signal, from first span to fleet policy.

docs.title: Wrap-up
docs.text:
You took a broken casino to a production-grade pipeline in three hours: SDK first, collector second, every fix verified in Dynatrace. Your Codespace and every config you wrote stay yours.

Fill in the session survey before you leave — and if you produce casino telemetry at work now, you know exactly which honeymoon you are ending.

docs.text: Goal: Codespace up, cluster healthy, Dynatrace connected, casino deployed, and you can play the casino. Budget 15 minutes; helpers circulate.

docs.title: 1. Start the Codespace
docs.text:
1. Open the training repository you received in your welcome email.
  2. Click Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main.
  3. Wait for post-create setup to finish — the terminal shows the kind cluster being created. Typically 3–5 minutes with a prebuild.

Your Codespace secrets were injected by the organizers. Check they are present:

env | grep -E 'DT_TENANT|DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN|DT_INGEST_TOKEN|PARTICIPANT_ID' | cut -d= -f1

Expected output: the four variable names (values stay hidden in lists):

DT_TENANT
DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN
DT_INGEST_TOKEN
PARTICIPANT_ID

Renamed from DT_API_TOKEN

The operator token is now DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN. If your Codespace secret is still named DT_API_TOKEN, bring-up continues (the installer accepts it as a deprecated fallback) — but rename the secret when you can. See the full contract in Environment variables below.

Your PARTICIPANT_ID is your identity

Everyone shares one Dynatrace tenant. PARTICIPANT_ID is the one value you set to be unique: it names your kind cluster and becomes k8s.cluster.name on every piece of telemetry you send. Keep it DNS-label-safe (lowercase letters, digits, - — no spaces or uppercase). Always filter Dynatrace by your cluster name — that is how you see your casino and not your neighbor's. (Advanced: KIND_CLUSTER_NAME overrides it if you ever need to name the cluster directly; most attendees never set it.)

Advanced track only: check opencode works

The advanced self-paced track drives the opencode AI coding agent, wired at start-up to a facilitator-hosted LLM proxy. If you are on that track and set the two WORKSHOP_* secrets, confirm the agent and its proxy credential are in place:

opencode --version                 # the CLI is baked into the image
test -f .workshop-llm.env && echo "proxy credential minted" || \
  echo "no proxy credential — re-run: bash .devcontainer/bootstrap/dispense-llm.sh"
opencode run "reply with the word READY"   # should return a model completion

No .workshop-llm.env? Post-create setup skipped the dispense because the WORKSHOP_* secrets were absent, or the dispenser was unreachable — see Troubleshooting. The M0–M5 modules do not need opencode, so you can ignore this on the main track.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
This is the one canonical contract for every variable the training consumes. .env.sample and .devcontainer/.env.example mirror it — if anything disagrees, this table wins.

Variable Type Consumed by Required? DT_TENANT Tenant base URL (https://<id>.live.dynatrace.com) Operator (<DT_TENANT>/api) and OTel collectors (<DT_TENANT>/api/v2/otlp) — one URL, two uses Required for all Dynatrace labs DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN Platform token (dt0s16), fleet-management:* + settings:objects:* scopes Dynatrace Operator → DynaKube apiToken (deploy/dynatrace/install.sh) Required for K8s monitoring (M4) DT_INGEST_TOKEN Platform token (dt0s16), openpipeline:{traces,metrics,logs,events}:ingest + storage:metrics:write Two consumers: OTel collectors' OTLP exporter (Bearer header) and operator dataIngestToken Required for telemetry export (M3/M5) DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN Platform token (dt0s16) dtctl only — never the operator Optional (dtctl labs) DT_PLATFORM_URL Gen3 SaaS apps URL (https://<id>.apps.dynatrace.com) dtctl on Gen3 SaaS Optional — derived from DT_TENANT when unset PARTICIPANT_ID DNS-label-safe id kind cluster name, k8s.cluster.name, DynaKube name Required (blank → otel-training, collides in a class) KIND_CLUSTER_NAME cluster name advanced override; wins over PARTICIPANT_ID Optional

The three DT_* tokens are all platform tokens but not interchangeable

On this Gen3 tenant DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN, DT_INGEST_TOKEN, and DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN are all platform tokens (dt0s16) — but each carries a different scope set and is minted separately: the operator token needs fleet-management:* + settings:objects:*, the ingest token needs openpipeline:*:ingest + storage:metrics:write, and DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN is used only by dtctl. Minting one where another is expected will fail auth. The old single DT_API_TOKEN is a deprecated alias for DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN only. (The Dynatrace Operator ≥ 1.10.0 is what accepts platform tokens in the apiToken/dataIngestToken Secret keys; install.sh pins 1.11.1.)

Two variables below are not Dynatrace tokens — they belong to the advanced track's opencode LLM dispenser (unrelated to the DT tenant):

Variable Type Consumed by Required? WORKSHOP_DISPENSER_URL URL dispense-llm.sh → opencode LLM proxy key Optional (advanced Step 1 only) WORKSHOP_ROOM_PASSWORD shared secret (X-Room-Password) dispense-llm.sh → dispenser auth Optional (advanced Step 1 only)

Davis CoPilot / OAuth (optional, not required)

If your cohort runs the optional Davis CoPilot exercise it uses a separate Dynatrace OAuth client (dt0s02), configured in its own advanced section — it is deliberately kept out of the required token set above. Most attendees do not need it.

Your lab mechanic for the whole session: edit a manifest → commit → Argo CD deploys it. No kubectl apply into the casino namespace (Argo CD's self-heal would revert it anyway).

All three UIs are forwarded to your codespace and appear, labelled, in the Ports panel (Casino app → 30000, Git host → 30001, Argo CD UI → 30002):

Endpoint URL Credentials Casino app http://localhost:30000 register a player in the UI Gitea (your Git host) http://localhost:30001 attendee / trainingpass123 Argo CD http://localhost:30002 admin / password printed at bootstrap

Using the external GitLab fork? When the GitOps bootstrap runs with GITOPS_PROVIDER=gitlab, the git host is not the in-cluster Gitea on 30001 — open your GitLab fork's web URL instead (printed in the GitOps bootstrap banner). Ports 30000 (casino) and 30002 (Argo CD) are unchanged.

docs.title: 5. Play the casino
docs.text:
The casino frontend (vegas-casino-frontend) is exposed through the Gateway API data plane on NodePort 30000 — no kubectl port-forward needed. In the Codespaces Ports panel it shows up labelled Casino app; click the globe icon on port 30000 (or open http://localhost:30000).

Open http://localhost:30000, register a player account, and play a few rounds — try the slots and another game. Any game works; the point is generating telemetry.

30000 is published by the kind control-plane node and forwarded to the codespace, the same way the Gitea (30001) and Argo CD (30002) UIs are.

Leave the casino open in a browser tab and use a terminal (+ icon) for everything else.

Sanity-check the entry point from inside the cluster:

  curl -fsS http://vegas-casino-frontend:3000/health

Expected: a health response from the frontend.

Every service exports OTLP to the gateway collector, which enriches and forwards to Dynatrace:

kubectl -n observability get otelcol
kubectl -n observability logs deploy/otel-gateway-collector --tail=5

Expected: otel-gateway and otel-logs both Running, no export errors in the gateway log.

docs.title: Catalog A1 — Fix a broken distributed trace
docs.text:
At a glance

Theme: traces · Time: 25 min · Difficulty: medium · Skill: otel-instrumentation · Reference: labs/advanced/catalog-a1-broken-trace/

Goal: a planted async hop between the slots and scoring services drops the trace context, so the distributed trace splits into two. You will use opencode with the otel-instrumentation skill to restore context propagation across the async boundary — and watch the trace reconnect end-to-end in Dynatrace. You run the Problem → Opencode → Verify loop, driving the agent with a numbered prompt ladder rather than one mega-prompt.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text: flowchart TB   subgraph before["Before — context dropped"]     s1["vegas-slots-servicePOST /spin"]     s2["casino.score.update(detached timer tick)"]     s3["vegas-scoring-servicePOST /score"]     s1 -. "trace ends here" .-> s2     s2 -. "NEW root trace" .-> s3   end   subgraph after["After — context restored"]     a1["vegas-slots-servicePOST /spin"] --> a2["casino.score.update(child span)"] --> a3["vegas-scoring-servicePOST /score"]   end

docs.title: ① Problem — the trace splits at the async hop
docs.text:
After a spin settles, the slots service records the result on vegas-scoring-service (SCORING_SERVICE_URL, port 8085). To keep /spin fast it does not await the call — it pushes a job onto an in-process queue drained by a setInterval timer. Planted state: labs/advanced/catalog-a1-broken-trace/before.slots-score-hop.js.

The break is subtle and extremely common: the drain tick is a fresh async context with no active span. OpenTelemetry context lives in Node's AsyncLocalStorage; it follows await chains inside one operation but does not flow into a setInterval/setTimeout callback. The HTTP client instrumentation only injects a traceparent header when a span is active in the current context — so the score call goes out header-less and scoring opens a brand-new root trace.

Confirm the symptom — run the checkpoint DQL now: scoring spans appear as parentless roots, and the /spin trace has no downstream scoring child.

docs.title: ② Understand the change
docs.text:
The fix is not "add a span" — it is carry the context across the async boundary. Two halves, both in the slots service:

  1. Capture context.active() at enqueue time, next to the payload.
  2. Restore it at drain time with context.with(...), and open an explicit casino.score.update child span, so the outgoing fetch has an active span to propagate from.

Target shape (after.slots-score-hop.js):

- scoreQueue.push({ player, game: 'slots', outcome: outcome.kind, payout });
+ scoreQueue.push({ job: { player, game: 'slots', outcome: outcome.kind, payout },
+                   ctx: context.active() });        // capture
  ...
- const job = scoreQueue.shift();
- await fetch(`${SCORING_URL}/score`, { ... });
+ const item = scoreQueue.shift();
+ await context.with(item.ctx, async () => {         // restore
+   const span = tracer.startSpan('casino.score.update', { attributes: { ... } });
+   await context.with(trace.setSpan(context.active(), span), async () => {
+     await fetch(`${SCORING_URL}/score`, { ... });  // traceparent now injected
+     span.end();
+   });
+ });

docs.title: ③ Drive opencode — the prompt ladder
docs.text:
Climb the ladder one rung at a time. After each rung, read what the agent did before you let it continue.

P1 · Orient (read-only)P2 · Core fixP3 · DeepenP4 · Steer 

Using the otel-instrumentation skill, read the slots service only — do not
edit yet. Where does /spin hand work to the scoring service, and in what
async context does the outgoing HTTP call actually run? Tell me why a
traceparent header would NOT be injected on that call.
What you should see: the agent identifies the setInterval drain loop and explains the call runs with no active span / no context. Review check: it names the detached timer tick as the cause — not "a missing span".

Now fix it: capture the active context where the score job is enqueued, and
restore it with context.with(...) in the drain loop before the fetch, so the
HTTP call propagates traceparent to vegas-scoring-service. Use
@opentelemetry/api. Keep /spin non-blocking.
What you should see: context.active() captured at enqueue; context.with wrapping the fetch at drain. Review check: /spin still returns before the score call runs.

Add an explicit child span 'casino.score.update' around the fetch, with
attributes casino.game.name, casino.outcome and peer.service =
vegas-scoring-service, and end it in a finally so errors still close it.
What you should see: a named client span wrapping the call, ended in finally. Review check: the span is created inside the restored context (so it is a child, not a new root).

Confirm the scoring call now inherits the /spin trace: show me that the span
is a child of the request context and that no new root trace is created for
the score update.
What you should see: the agent reasons that trace.setSpan on the restored context makes the hop a child of the spin. Review check: no context.active() is captured inside the timer (that would re-root it).

docs.title: ④ Review & apply
docs.text:
Read the diff against after.slots-score-hop.js, then ship via GitOps:

git add . && git commit -m "fix(slots): propagate trace context across the scoring hop"
git push            # to your fork's main — Argo CD syncs the slots service

Play a few rounds of slots so new traces flow.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run in a Grail Notebook, filtered to your cluster.

Before — scoring spans are parentless roots (this should collapse to ~0):

fetch spans, from: now() - 30m
| filter service.name == "vegas-scoring-service" and endpoint.name == "POST /score"
| filter isNull(span.parent_id)
| summarize orphan_roots = count(), by: { bin(timestamp, 1m) }

After — slots and scoring share one trace (reconnected end-to-end):

fetch spans, from: now() - 30m
| filter span.name == "casino.score.update"
| fieldsAdd has_parent = isNotNull(span.parent_id)
| summarize reconnected = countIf(has_parent == true), by: { bin(timestamp, 1m) }
  • Before: orphan_roots is non-zero; reconnected is empty — the trace is split.
  • After: orphan_roots drops to zero and reconnected climbs — opening any /spin trace now shows casino.score.update → vegas-scoring-service as children of the spin.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

  • Adds a span but no context carry (trace still splits): "the fix must capture context.active() at enqueue and restore it with context.with before the fetch — a span alone does not cross the setInterval boundary."
  • Captures context inside the timer tick: "capturing context inside the drain loop re-roots the trace — capture it where the job is enqueued."
  • Makes /spin await the score call: "keep /spin non-blocking; the hop stays asynchronous, we only carry the context into it."

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• Context captured at enqueue and restored with context.with at drain
  • A casino.score.update child span wraps the scoring call, ended in finally
  • orphan_roots DQL drops to zero after the fix
  • A /spin trace shows casino.score.update → vegas-scoring-service as children

Back to the catalog menu.

docs.title: Catalog A2 — Log ↔ trace correlation
docs.text:
At a glance

Theme: traces / logs · Time: 20 min · Difficulty: medium · Skill: otel-instrumentation · Reference: labs/advanced/catalog-a2-log-trace-correlation/

Goal: the slots service logs each spin as a structured JSON line, but the line carries no trace context — so in Dynatrace a log record and the span it was emitted during are unlinked. You will use opencode with the otel-instrumentation skill to inject trace_id / span_id into every log line, then watch Dynatrace pivot from a slow /spin trace straight to its logs — and back. You run the Problem → Opencode → Verify loop, driving the agent with a numbered prompt ladder rather than one mega-prompt.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text: flowchart TB   subgraph before["Before — two unlinked panes"]     tb["Trace: POST /spincasino.slots.spin"]     lb["Log: 'spin settled'(no trace_id)"]     tb -. "no link" .- lb   end   subgraph after["After — one click between them"]     ta["Trace: POST /spincasino.slots.spin"]     la["Log: 'spin settled'trace_id + span_id"]     ta <--> la   end

docs.title: ① Problem — the log line has no trace context
docs.text:
After a spin settles, the slots service writes a structured JSON log line to stdout — scraped by the DaemonSet filelog collector and shipped to Dynatrace. Planted state: labs/advanced/catalog-a2-log-trace-correlation/before.slots-logger.js. The line is emitted while the casino.slots.spin span is active, yet it records none of that span's identity:

{ "timestamp": "…", "level": "info", "message": "spin settled",
  "service.name": "vegas-slots-service", "casino.outcome": "jackpot" }

No trace_id, no span_id. In Dynatrace the log and the span live in two separate panes with nothing linking them: opening a slow /spin trace cannot pivot to "the logs for THIS request", and a suspicious log line cannot jump to the trace that produced it.

Confirm the symptom — run the checkpoint DQL now: the share of slots log records with a trace_id is zero.

docs.title: ② Understand the change
docs.text:
The fix is to read the active span's SpanContext and stamp its ids onto every log line. Two facts make this work:

  1. trace_id and span_id are the OpenTelemetry log data-model trace-context fields. Dynatrace correlates a log record to a span when they are present — no extra configuration.
  2. A logger that writes plain JSON to stdout does not attach them automatically. You read them from trace.getSpan(context.active()).spanContext() and inject them yourself.

Target shape (after.slots-logger.js):

+ const { trace, context } = require('@opentelemetry/api');

  function log(level, message, fields = {}) {
+   const span = trace.getSpan(context.active());
+   const sc = span && span.spanContext();
+   const correlation = sc
+     ? { trace_id: sc.traceId, span_id: sc.spanId, trace_flags: sc.traceFlags }
+     : {};
    process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify({
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(), level, message,
      'service.name': 'vegas-slots-service',
+     ...correlation,
      ...fields,
    }) + '\n');
  }

Use the standard keys, top-level

The correlation keys Dynatrace recognises are the lower-snake-case trace_id / span_id, as top-level fields on the log record. Nesting them under an object, or renaming to traceId / dt.trace_id, breaks the link. When no span is active, omit the fields — never log a fabricated or all-zero id.

docs.title: ③ Drive opencode — the prompt ladder
docs.text:
Climb the ladder one rung at a time. After each rung, read what the agent did before you let it continue.

P1 · Orient (read-only)P2 · Core fixP3 · DeepenP4 · Steer 

Using the otel-instrumentation skill, read the slots service logger only — do
not edit. The service logs each spin while a casino.slots.spin span is active,
yet the log line has no trace_id. Explain why Dynatrace cannot link that log
record to its span.
What you should see: the agent identifies that the logger never reads the active span context, so the ids are absent from the record. Review check: it names trace_id / span_id as the missing correlation fields — not "a missing log attribute" in general.

Now fix it: read the active span's SpanContext via
trace.getSpan(context.active()) and inject trace_id, span_id and trace_flags
as top-level fields on every structured log line. Use @opentelemetry/api.
If no span is active, omit the fields — do not log zeros.
What you should see: trace.getSpan(context.active()) read inside the log helper; the three ids spread onto the JSON object. Review check: the keys are exactly trace_id / span_id (snake_case), top-level — not nested, not camelCase.

Make it safe: when there is no active span (startup, background ticks) the
line must still be valid JSON with no correlation keys. Confirm trace_flags is
included so sampled/unsampled is visible on the record.
What you should see: a guarded branch that omits the ids when no span is active; trace_flags present when one is. Review check: no all-zero 00000000... id is ever emitted.

Confirm the correlation keys match what Dynatrace expects: top-level trace_id
and span_id in lower snake_case. Show me they are NOT nested under an object
and NOT renamed to traceId / dt.trace_id.
What you should see: the agent re-reads the emitted object and confirms the key names and placement. Review check: the ids survive as top-level fields after ...fields spread (a later field cannot clobber them).

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run in a Grail Notebook, filtered to your cluster.

Share of slots logs carrying a trace id (climbs from 0 toward 1.0):

fetch logs, from: now() - 30m
| filter service.name == "vegas-slots-service"
| fieldsAdd correlated = isNotNull(trace_id)
| summarize correlated = countIf(correlated == true), total = count(), by: { bin(timestamp, 1m) }
| fieldsAdd ratio = correlated / total

The pivot that proves it — pick one spin's trace_id and fetch its logs:

fetch logs, from: now() - 30m
| filter service.name == "vegas-slots-service" and isNotNull(trace_id)
| fields timestamp, trace_id, span_id, content
| sort timestamp desc
| limit 20
  • Before: ratio is 0 — every slots log is orphaned from its trace.
  • After: ratio climbs toward 1.0, and in the trace view opening any /spin trace now shows a Logs tab scoped to that trace_id — one click from span to the exact lines it produced, and the log view links back to the trace.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

  • Logs the ids nested or renamed ({ otel: { traceId } }, dt.trace_id): "the correlation keys are top-level trace_id and span_id in lower snake_case — Dynatrace does not recognise nested or camelCase variants."
  • Reads the span at module load, not per-call: "read the active span inside the log function, per line — the active span changes every request."
  • Emits an all-zero id when no span is active: "omit the correlation keys entirely when there is no active span; never log an all-zero trace_id."
  • Puts ...correlation after ...fields: "spread correlation last-ish but ensure a caller field cannot overwrite trace_id/span_id."

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• trace_id, span_id, trace_flags injected as top-level log fields
  • Ids read from the active span per log call (not at module load)
  • No correlation keys (and no all-zero ids) when no span is active
  • ratio DQL climbs toward 1.0 after the fix
  • Opening a /spin trace in Dynatrace shows its logs scoped to that trace_id

docs.title: Catalog A3 — Multi-language instrumentation
docs.text:
At a glance

Theme: traces · Time: 25 min · Difficulty: medium · Skill: otel-instrumentation · Reference: labs/advanced/catalog-a3-multi-language/

Goal: Step 1 instrumented slots in JavaScript. Here you apply the same span pattern to a second SDK — the Python roulette service — proving the casino.* semantic-convention contract is language-agnostic. You will use opencode with the otel-instrumentation skill to open a casino.roulette.spin span carrying the identical attribute names slots uses, then watch one DQL answer both games. You run the Problem → Opencode → Verify loop, driving the agent with a numbered prompt ladder rather than one mega-prompt.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
flowchart LR subgraph js["slots — JavaScript (Step 1)"] j["casino.slots.spincasino.game.name, casino.outcome,casino.payout.amount"] end subgraph py["roulette — Python (this exercise)"] p["casino.roulette.spincasino.game.name, casino.outcome,casino.payout.amount"] end j --> contract{{"same attribute NAMES(Weaver registry)"}} p --> contract contract --> dql["one DQL / one dashboardanswers BOTH games"]

Target choice — roulette (Python) or dice (Go)

This page uses the Python roulette service. The Go dice service is the equivalent alternative: same attributes, go.opentelemetry.io/otel instead of the Python SDK, tracer.Start(ctx, "casino.dice.roll"). Pick whichever SDK you want the practice in — the contract is identical.

docs.title: ① Problem — roulette is invisible to the money-path DQL
docs.text:
Slots (Step 1) emits a casino.slots.spin span with casino.game.name, casino.bet.amount, casino.outcome and casino.payout.amount, so Dynatrace can slice the money path by game / outcome / payout. The Python roulette service runs every spin under a generic http_request span only — no domain span, none of the casino.* attributes. Planted state: labs/advanced/catalog-a3-multi-language/before.roulette-spin.py.

Confirm the symptom — run the checkpoint DQL now: there is no casino.roulette.spin span, and roulette does not appear in any casino.outcome roll-up.

docs.title: ② Understand the change
docs.text:
The fix is not new conventions for Python — it is the same contract, ported. Open an explicit casino.roulette.spin child span and set the identical attribute names slots uses (only the values differ: roulette vs slots). Mapping across the two SDKs:

JavaScript (Step 1) Python (this exercise) trace.getTracer('casino-slots', '1.0.0') trace.get_tracer("casino-roulette", "2.1.0") tracer.startActiveSpan('casino.slots.spin', fn) with tracer.start_as_current_span("casino.roulette.spin") span.setAttribute('casino.game.name', 'slots') spin.set_attribute("casino.game.name", "roulette") span.setStatus({ code: ERROR }) spin.set_status(StatusCode.ERROR, …)

Target shape (after.roulette-spin.py):

+ from opentelemetry import trace
+ from opentelemetry.trace import StatusCode
+ tracer = trace.get_tracer("casino-roulette", "2.1.0")

  def _handle_spin(self, span=None):
      if span: add_http_attributes(span, "POST", "/spin")
      data = self._read_body()
-     winning_number = random.randint(0, 36)
-     payout = calculate_payout(bet_type, data.get("BetValue"), winning_number)
-     self._send_json_response({ ... })
+     with tracer.start_as_current_span("casino.roulette.spin") as spin:
+         spin.set_attribute("casino.game.name", "roulette")
+         spin.set_attribute("casino.bet.amount", data.get("BetAmount", 0))
+         winning_number = random.randint(0, 36)
+         payout = calculate_payout(bet_type, data.get("BetValue"), winning_number)
+         outcome = "win" if payout > 0 else "lose"
+         spin.set_attribute("casino.outcome", outcome)
+         spin.set_attribute("casino.payout.amount", payout)
+         self._send_json_response({ ... })

The names are the contract

Diverge the attribute names (game, bet_amount, casino.roulette.outcome) and you get two of everything — two dashboard tiles, two DQL filters — and nothing rolls up. Matching slots exactly means Step 3's Weaver registry check guards roulette too, and the whole casino answers one query.

docs.text:

Add an explicit casino.roulette.spin child span around the draw and payout,
using tracer.start_as_current_span. Set casino.game.name='roulette',
casino.bet.amount, casino.outcome and casino.payout.amount — the SAME attribute
names the slots service uses. Keep it a child of the http_request span.
What you should see: a with tracer.start_as_current_span(...) block wrapping the settlement, with the four casino.* attributes. Review check: the attribute names match slots exactly; only values differ (roulette).

Make the span honest on failure: set status ERROR and record_exception on an
error, and re-raise. Add a jackpot event when payout is a 30x+ win, matching
the slots jackpot event.
What you should see: set_status(StatusCode.ERROR, ...) + record_exception in an except, and an add_event("jackpot", ...). Review check: the with context-manager ends the span automatically (no manual end() needed, unlike a bare start_span).

Confirm the roulette span rolls up with slots: show me that a single DQL
filtering casino.outcome returns BOTH games, and that the Weaver registry from
Step 2/3 would accept casino.roulette.spin without new attribute definitions.
What you should see: the agent reasons that identical names mean one query covers both, and no registry change is needed. Review check: no attribute was renamed into a roulette-specific namespace.

docs.text:
Read the diff against after.roulette-spin.py, then ship via GitOps:

git add . && git commit -m "feat(roulette): add casino.roulette.spin span matching the slots contract"
git push            # to your fork's main — Argo CD syncs the roulette service

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run in a Grail Notebook, filtered to your cluster.

Roulette now emits the domain span (was empty before):

fetch spans, from: now() - 30m
| filter span.name == "casino.roulette.spin"
| summarize spins = count(), by: { casino.outcome }

The cross-language roll-up — one query, both SDKs, by game:

fetch spans, from: now() - 30m
| filter isNotNull(casino.game.name)
| summarize spins = count(), by: { casino.game.name, casino.outcome }
  • Before: casino.roulette.spin returns nothing; the roll-up shows only slots.
  • After: roulette appears alongside slots under the same casino.game.name / casino.outcome dimensions — one DQL, one dashboard tile, both languages. The contract crossed the SDK boundary.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

  • Invents Python-specific names (game, casino.roulette.outcome): "match the slots attribute names exactly — casino.game.name, casino.outcome — only the value changes to 'roulette'."
  • Uses start_span without a context manager (span never ends): "use with tracer.start_as_current_span(...) so the span ends and becomes a child of http_request."
  • Makes it a new root instead of a child: "start the span inside the active http_request context so it is a child, not a second root trace."
  • Skips error status: "set status ERROR and record_exception on failure, then re-raise — the span must reflect the outcome."

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• casino.roulette.spin child span wraps the draw + payout settlement
  • Attribute names (casino.game.name / .bet.amount / .outcome / .payout.amount) match slots exactly
  • Span ended via with context-manager; ERROR status + record_exception on failure
  • casino.roulette.spin DQL returns data after the fix
  • The cross-language roll-up shows both slots and roulette under one query

docs.title: Catalog B1 — RED metrics from spans
docs.text:
At a glance

Theme: metrics / collector · Time: 20 min · Difficulty: medium · Skill: otel-collector · Reference: labs/advanced/catalog-b1-spanmetrics/

Goal: get RED metrics — Rate, Errors, Duration — for every casino operation without touching application code, by adding the spanmetrics connector to the gateway collector. You drive opencode with the otel-collector skill through a prompt ladder, then chart the result.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
flowchart LR spans["Span stream(all services)"] --> conn["spanmetricsconnector"] conn --> calls["casino.red.calls(Rate + Errors)"] conn --> dur["casino.red.duration(Duration histogram)"] calls --> dt["Dynatrace"] dur --> dt

A connector is both an exporter and a receiver: it consumes the trace pipeline's spans and produces a metrics stream. You get RED for free from telemetry you are already sending — no SDK change, no redeploy of the casino services.

docs.title: ① Problem — rich traces, no RED rollup
docs.text: The casino emits detailed spans, but there is no cheap aggregate of request rate, error rate, or latency distribution per operation. Answering "what is the p90 of POST /spin and how many are erroring per minute?" means scanning spans — expensive and slow for a dashboard or SLO. Confirm it: run the checkpoint DQL for casino.red.calls now — no such metric.

docs.title: ② Understand the change
docs.text:
Add the spanmetrics connector to observability/collectors/gateway.yaml (reference: labs/advanced/catalog-b1-spanmetrics/spanmetrics-connector.yaml). It is wired as an exporter on the traces pipeline and a receiver on a new metrics pipeline:

connectors:
  spanmetrics:
    histogram:
      explicit:
        buckets: [1ms, 5ms, 10ms, 25ms, 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2s, 5s]
    dimensions:
      - name: casino.game.name
      - name: casino.outcome
    namespace: casino.red
    aggregation_temporality: AGGREGATION_TEMPORALITY_DELTA   # match tenant delta convention
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      exporters: [otlphttp/dynatrace, spanmetrics]   # feed the connector too
    metrics/spanmetrics:
      receivers: [spanmetrics]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]            # invariants hold here
      exporters: [otlphttp/dynatrace]

RED maps to: casino.red.calls (rate), the same metric split by status.code (errors), and casino.red.duration (duration histogram). Keep the dimensions bounded — span.name, status.code, and the two casino dims — never player.id/round.id.

Delta temporality

The baseline metrics pipeline converts counters to delta via cumulativetodelta, but connector output does not pass through it. Set aggregation_temporality: AGGREGATION_TEMPORALITY_DELTA on the connector so casino.red.* follows the tenant's delta convention instead of shipping cumulative.

docs.title: ③ Drive opencode — the prompt ladder
docs.text:
P1 · Orient (read-only)P2 · Core — add the connectorP3 · Deepen — dimensions + bucketsP4 · Steer — verify the wiring 

Using the otel-collector skill, read observability/collectors/gateway.yaml —
do not edit. List the current pipelines and their exporters, and tell me
where a spanmetrics connector would attach to derive RED metrics from spans.
What you should see: the agent maps the traces pipeline and names the connector attach points (traces exporter + new metrics receiver). Review check: it does not propose any application-code change.

Add a spanmetrics connector under a connectors: block with namespace
casino.red and a duration histogram. Wire it as an exporter on the traces
pipeline and as the receiver of a new metrics/spanmetrics pipeline that
exports to Dynatrace.
What you should see: a connectors: block plus the two pipeline edits. Review check: the new metrics pipeline keeps memory_limiter first and batch last.

Add dimensions casino.game.name and casino.outcome to the connector, and set
explicit histogram buckets from 1ms to 5s. Do NOT add player.id or round.id.
What you should see: bounded dimensions: and an explicit.buckets list. Review check: no unbounded per-player/per-round dimension slipped in.

Confirm the connector is both an exporter (traces) and a receiver
(metrics/spanmetrics), and that the invariants hold on every pipeline:
memory_limiter first, batch last.
What you should see: the agent re-reads the service block and confirms both attachments and the invariant order. Review check: the traces pipeline still exports to Dynatrace and spanmetrics — not one or the other.

docs.title: ④ Review & apply
docs.text:
Diff against the reference, then apply the collector:

kubectl apply -f observability/collectors/gateway.yaml
kubectl -n observability rollout status deploy/otel-gateway-collector

Drive some load (the k6 loadgen is already running) so spans flow through the connector.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
// R + E — call rate per operation, with error isolation
timeseries calls = sum(casino.red.calls), by: { span.name, status.code }, from: now() - 1h

// D — p90 request duration per operation
timeseries d_p90 = percentile(casino.red.duration, 90), by: { span.name }, from: now() - 1h
  • Before: casino.red.* does not exist — both queries return nothing.
  • After: casino.red.calls returns a series per span.name (× status.code, so errors are isolated), and casino.red.duration returns a p90 per operation — a full RED view, built entirely at the collector.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

  • Puts spanmetrics on the metrics receiver side only: "spanmetrics is a connector — it must be an exporter on the traces pipeline AND the receiver of the new metrics pipeline."
  • Drops the Dynatrace exporter from traces: "the traces pipeline must keep exporting to Dynatrace as well as feeding spanmetrics."
  • Adds unbounded dimensions: "only span.name, status.code, casino.game.name and casino.outcome — no player.id or round.id."
  • Breaks the invariant: "memory_limiter must be first and batch last on the new metrics/spanmetrics pipeline."

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• spanmetrics connector added with namespace: casino.red and a duration histogram
  • Wired as traces exporter + metrics/spanmetrics pipeline receiver
  • Invariants hold on every pipeline (memory_limiter first, batch last)
  • casino.red.calls and casino.red.duration return data in Grail
  • No casino application code changed
