docs.title: Catalog B3 — Drop noise (filter processor)
docs.text:
At a glance

Theme: metrics / collector · Time: 15 min · Difficulty: easy · Skill: otel-collector · Reference: labs/advanced/catalog-b3-filter-drop-noise/

Goal: health-check and /metrics scrape spans fire every few seconds on every pod — pure volume with no diagnostic signal that inflates ingest cost and buries the money-path traces. You will use opencode with the otel-collector skill to add a filter processor to the gateway that drops them before export, then verify the noise collapses while real /spin spans keep flowing. You run the Problem → Opencode → Verify loop, driving the agent with a numbered prompt ladder rather than one mega-prompt.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
flowchart LR spans["Span stream(all services)"] --> ml["memory_limiter"] ml --> k8s["k8sattributes"] k8s --> f["filter/drop_noisehealth · /metrics · probes"] f -->|"/spin, /score …"| b["batch"] f -. "dropped" .-x drop(("✗")) b --> dt["Dynatrace"]

The filter processor evaluates an OTTL condition per span: match a health/scrape span and drop it here, so Dynatrace never ingests (or bills for) it.

docs.title: ① Problem — scrape noise drowns the signal
docs.text: Every pod answers liveness/readiness probes (/health, /healthz, /readyz) and a Prometheus scrape (/metrics) on a tight interval. Each becomes a span. They carry no diagnostic value — but they dominate span volume, inflate ingest cost, and make the trace list a wall of /health. Confirm it: run the checkpoint DQL now — health/scrape spans are a large, steady share of ingest.

docs.title: ② Understand the change
docs.text:
Add a filter processor to observability/collectors/gateway.yaml (reference: labs/advanced/catalog-b3-filter-drop-noise/filter-drop-noise-processor.yaml) and wire it onto the traces pipeline between k8sattributes and batch:

processors:
  filter/drop_noise:
    error_mode: ignore          # a span missing an attr => "no match", not an error
    traces:
      span:
        # DROP when ANY condition is true (OTTL):
        - 'attributes["http.route"] == "/health"'
        - 'attributes["http.route"] == "/healthz"'
        - 'attributes["http.route"] == "/readyz"'
        - 'attributes["http.route"] == "/metrics"'
        - 'IsMatch(attributes["url.path"], "^/(health|healthz|readyz|metrics)$")'
        - 'IsMatch(attributes["user_agent.original"], "^(kube-probe|Prometheus)/.*")'
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, filter/drop_noise, batch]

Invariants still hold

memory_limiter stays first (it must sit ahead of anything that fans out work) and batch stays last (nothing drops spans after they are batched for export). The filter slots between them — right after enrichment, so a dropped span never reaches batch. Only the traces pipeline changes; metrics and logs are untouched.

Prefer http.route over url.path

http.route is the SDK-normalised, low-cardinality template (/health), so match on it when present. url.path is the raw request path — the regex fallback covers SDKs that only set that. Matching the route avoids accidentally dropping a real endpoint that merely contains "health" in a query string.

docs.title: ③ Drive opencode — the prompt ladder
docs.text:
Climb the ladder one rung at a time. After each rung, read what the agent did before you let it continue.

P1 · Orient (read-only)P2 · Core — add the filterP3 · Deepen — robust matchingP4 · Steer — prove no over-drop 

Using the otel-collector skill, read observability/collectors/gateway.yaml —
do not edit. List the traces pipeline processors in order, and tell me where a
filter processor that drops health-check and /metrics spans must go so the
memory_limiter-first / batch-last invariants still hold.
What you should see: the agent names the traces pipeline order and places the filter between k8sattributes and batch. Review check: it does not propose dropping spans at the app or after batch.

Add a filter/drop_noise processor that DROPS spans whose http.route is
/health, /healthz, /readyz or /metrics. Use error_mode: ignore. Wire it onto
the traces pipeline between k8sattributes and batch. Do not touch metrics or
logs.
What you should see: a filter/drop_noise block with traces.span conditions, added to the traces pipeline in the right position. Review check: memory_limiter first, batch last, filter in between.

Make matching robust: add a url.path regex fallback for SDKs that only set the
raw path, and drop spans whose user_agent.original starts with kube-probe/ or
Prometheus/. Keep health-named real endpoints safe by preferring http.route.
What you should see: IsMatch conditions on url.path and user_agent.original alongside the route checks. Review check: the conditions anchor the regex (^…$) so they don't match a real path that merely contains "health".

Confirm the filter drops ONLY noise: POST /spin and POST /score spans must
still flow. Re-read the traces pipeline and confirm the invariant order, and
that metrics/logs pipelines are unchanged.
What you should see: the agent re-reads the service block and confirms /spin is unaffected and the order holds. Review check: no condition matches an operational endpoint; metrics/logs pipelines untouched.

docs.title: ④ Review & apply
docs.text:
Diff against the reference, then apply the collector:

kubectl apply -f observability/collectors/gateway.yaml
kubectl -n observability rollout status deploy/otel-gateway-collector

The k6 loadgen and the kubelet probes keep running, so both signal and noise flow — you will see the noise drop within a minute.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run in a Grail Notebook, filtered to your cluster.

Noise — health/scrape spans reaching Dynatrace (collapses toward zero):

fetch spans, from: now() - 30m
| filter matchesPhrase(endpoint.name, "health") or matchesPhrase(endpoint.name, "metrics")
| summarize noise = count(), by: { bin(timestamp, 1m) }

Signal — real operations still flow (must stay non-zero — the over-drop guard):

fetch spans, from: now() - 30m
| filter endpoint.name == "POST /spin" or endpoint.name == "POST /score"
| summarize operations = count(), by: { bin(timestamp, 1m) }
  • Before: noise is a large, steady band; it dwarfs the operational spans.
  • After: noise drops to ~0 at the moment the collector rolls out, while operations is unchanged — you removed volume, not signal.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

  • Drops a real endpoint (/spin disappears): "the filter must match only health/metrics/probe spans — anchor the regex and prefer http.route so operational endpoints are never dropped."
  • Breaks the invariant (filter after batch, or memory_limiter not first): "memory_limiter first, batch last; the filter goes between k8sattributes and batch."
  • Edits the metrics or logs pipeline: "only the traces pipeline changes — leave metrics and logs untouched."
  • Omits error_mode: ignore (spans missing the attr error the batch): "set error_mode: ignore so a span without http.route evaluates as no-match instead of failing."

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• filter/drop_noise processor drops /health, /healthz, /readyz, /metrics spans
  • Wired on the traces pipeline between k8sattributes and batch
  • Invariants hold (memory_limiter first, batch last); metrics/logs untouched
  • noise DQL collapses to ~0 after apply
  • operations DQL (/spin, /score) is unchanged — no signal loss

Back to the catalog menu.

docs.title: Catalog C1 — Build a Dynatrace dashboard via dtctl
docs.text:
At a glance

Theme: Dynatrace automation · Time: 20 min · Difficulty: medium · Skill: dtctl · Reference: labs/advanced/catalog-c1-dtctl-dashboard/

Goal: turn the business metrics you built in Step 2 (and the Catalog B1 RED metrics) into a live Dynatrace dashboard — as code. You drive opencode with the dtctl skill through a prompt ladder; no clicking in the UI.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text: flowchart LR   m["Step-2 metricscasino.bets.countcasino.wager.amountcasino.red.*"] --> oc["opencode(dtctl skill)"]   oc --> doc["dashboard document(24-col grid JSON)"]   doc --> v["dtctl apply -f … --dry-run(validate)"]   v --> dt["dtctl apply -f …→ Dynatrace"]

docs.title: ① Problem — the metrics exist, but no one is watching them
docs.text: After Step 2 and B1 the casino emits first-class business and RED metrics, but there is no dashboard — nobody can see bets-per-minute, wager p90, or error rate at a glance. A dashboard clicked together in the UI is invisible to review and impossible to reproduce per attendee. You want it as a document applied with dtctl: version controlled, diffable, deployed from the same codespace.

docs.title: ② Understand the change
docs.text:
You produce a dashboard document (reference: labs/advanced/catalog-c1-dtctl-dashboard/casino-business-dashboard.json) on a 24-column grid, with tiles built on DQL over your metrics, and deploy it with dtctl apply -f <file> — running --dry-run first, which validates schema and DQL before anything ships (fail-closed). dtctl is kubectl-style (apply / verify / get over a resource); there is no dtctl dashboard verb group, and the dashboard's identity comes from the name field in the document body, not a --name flag. This mirrors the mandatory dt-app-dashboards discipline: define purpose → explore the data → validate DQL → construct the JSON → deploy.

Tile DQL Reads Bets per minute by outcome timeseries sum(casino.bets.count), by:{casino.outcome} Step 2 counter Wager p90 by game timeseries percentile(casino.wager.amount, 90), by:{casino.game.name} Step 2 histogram RED — call rate timeseries sum(casino.red.calls), by:{span.name, status.code} B1 spanmetrics RED — p90 duration timeseries percentile(casino.red.duration, 90), by:{span.name} B1 spanmetrics

dtctl authenticates with the platform token already in your codespace (ISI-7175) — no extra secret.

docs.title: ③ Drive opencode — the prompt ladder
docs.text:
P1 · Orient (read-only)P2 · Core — build the documentP3 · Deepen — header + single valueP4 · Steer — validate then deploy 

Using the dtctl skill, list the metrics available to me that match
casino.bets.*, casino.wager.* and casino.red.* — and show the DQL you would
use to chart each. Do not create a dashboard yet.
What you should see: the agent runs dtctl to confirm the metrics exist and drafts one timeseries query per tile. Review check: every query references a metric that actually returns data.

Create a dashboard document on a 24-column grid with four tiles: bets per
minute by casino.outcome, wager p90 by casino.game.name, RED call rate by
span.name and status.code, and RED p90 duration by span.name. Use the DQL
from P1.
What you should see: a JSON document with tiles + layouts on a 24-wide grid. Review check: tiles do not overlap and fit within 24 columns.

Add a markdown header tile across the top and a single-value tile for total
wagered in the last hour. Set the dashboard's name field in the document body
to include my PARTICIPANT_ID (dtctl takes identity from the document, not a
flag).
What you should see: a markdown tile at row 0, a singleValue tile, and a top-level name field in the JSON. Review check: the name is in the document body — not passed as a --name flag (which apply ignores).

Validate the document with `dtctl apply -f <file> --dry-run` before deploying,
and only run the real `dtctl apply -f <file>` if the dry-run passes. Show me
the dry-run output.
What you should see: dtctl apply -f … --dry-run runs clean (fail-closed on bad schema/DQL), then dtctl apply -f … deploys. Review check: the agent uses dtctl apply -f (kubectl-style) — not a non-existent dtctl dashboard command — and refuses to deploy if the dry-run fails.

docs.title: ④ Review & apply
docs.text:
Diff against the reference document, then deploy (the manual equivalent of what opencode runs):

bash labs/advanced/catalog-c1-dtctl-dashboard/dtctl-apply.sh

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
• Open Dynatrace → Dashboards and find ${PARTICIPANT_ID}-business-overview.
  • Each tile renders data: bets-by-outcome trends, a wager-p90 bar per game, the RED call-rate and duration charts.
  • Re-run dtctl apply -f … --dry-run — it exits 0 (schema + DQL valid).

Confirm the queries resolve directly in a Notebook:

timeseries bets = sum(casino.bets.count), by: { casino.outcome }, from: now() - 1h
  • Before: no dashboard — the operator view does not exist.
  • After: a versioned, reproducible dashboard renders the casino's business and RED health, deployed entirely from code.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

  • Applies without validating: "always run dtctl apply -f … --dry-run first and only deploy if it passes."
  • Reaches for a dtctl dashboard command: "dtctl is kubectl-style — use dtctl apply -f <file>, there is no dtctl dashboard verb group."
  • Invents metric or field names: "only use metrics that P1 confirmed return data — do not guess field names."
  • Tiles overflow the grid: "the grid is 24 columns wide; keep tile x + w ≤ 24 and avoid overlaps."
  • Hardcodes a tenant or token: "dtctl uses the platform token in the environment — do not embed credentials in the document."

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• Dashboard document built on the 24-column grid from Step-2 + B1 metrics
  • All DQL validated (dtctl apply -f … --dry-run exits 0)
  • Deployed with dtctl apply -f …; dashboard name in the document body includes PARTICIPANT_ID
  • Every tile renders data in Dynatrace
  • No credentials embedded in the document

Back to the catalog menu.

docs.title: Catalog — extra exercises (choose your path)
docs.text:
Beyond the linear Step 0–7 arc, the catalog holds self-contained exercises — grouped by theme — that a facilitator can drop in for depth or variety. Each follows the same teaching shape as the main arc: ① Problem → ② Understand the change → ③ opencode prompt ladder → ④ Review & apply → ⑤ Verify (DQL), with a planted labs/advanced/… reference answer.

Themes: A = traces/instrumentation · B = metrics/collector · C = Dynatrace automation. Pick by the time you have and the muscle you want to build:

Exercise Theme Time Difficulty opencode skill You will… A1 — Fix a broken distributed trace traces 25m med otel-instrumentation Restore context propagation across a dropped async hop so the slots → scoring trace reconnects end-to-end. A2 — Log ↔ trace correlation traces / logs 20m med otel-instrumentation Inject trace_id / span_id into slots logs so Dynatrace links each log line to its span — and pivots between them. A3 — Multi-language instrumentation traces 25m med otel-instrumentation Port the Step-1 span pattern to a 2nd SDK (Python roulette), proving the casino.* contract crosses languages. B1 — RED metrics from spans metrics / collector 20m med otel-collector Add the spanmetrics connector to the gateway and chart Rate / Errors / Duration — no app-code change. B3 — Drop noise (filter processor) metrics / collector 15m easy otel-collector Drop health-check / /metrics spans at the gateway — verify the ingest drop with no signal loss. C1 — Build a dashboard via dtctl Dynatrace automation 20m med dtctl Turn your Step-2 business metrics into a live, version-controlled Dynatrace dashboard — as code.

Prerequisites

All assume the base environment is up and Step 0 — Warmup has installed the opencode skills (opencode debug skill lists otel-* and dtctl). A2 and A3 build on the span pattern from Step 1; C1 builds on the metrics from Step 2 and the RED metrics from B1.

docs.title: The environment
docs.text: Goal: understand the five moving parts of your lab — the casino app, GitLab, Argo CD, and the OTel Operator + collectors — then open Dynatrace and see the planted issues you will fix across steps 1–7. This page also introduces the one pattern you reuse on every step: the Problem → Opencode → Verify loop. Budget 15 minutes.

docs.title: The shape of the lab
docs.text:
Everything runs in one kind cluster inside your Codespace. Your GitLab fork is the single source of truth; Argo CD deploys whatever is committed there; the OTel Operator manages the collectors that enrich your telemetry and forward it to Dynatrace.

flowchart LR you["attendee"] -->|commit to fork| gitlab["GitLab forkk8s/ manifests"] gitlab -->|HTTPS poll| argo["Argo CD"] argo -->|sync + selfHeal| casino["casino namespacefrontend, scoring, slots,roulette, dice, blackjack"] operator["OTel Operator"] -->|manages| gw["otel-gateway-collector"] operator -->|manages| logs["otel-logs DaemonSet"] casino -. "OTLP gRPC/HTTP" .-> gw logs -. "pod logs" .-> gw gw -->|OTLP/HTTP| dt[("Dynatrace tenant")]

docs.title: Who does what
docs.text: Component Namespace Role in the lab Casino services casino Frontend + per-game services (slots, roulette, dice, blackjack) + scoring, Redis, PostgreSQL, k6 load-gen. The thing you are observing. GitLab fork external Holds the Kubernetes manifests under k8s/. You edit here. Argo CD argocd Polls your fork and applies it. selfHeal reverts hand-drift. OTel Operator observability Manages the gateway collector and the logs DaemonSet as CRDs. Gateway collector observability The single control point. All collector fixes in steps 4–7 land here. Dynatrace Operator dynatrace Kubernetes monitoring + ActiveGate.

docs.title: The lab mechanic: edit → commit → sync
docs.text:
Your loop for the whole track:

  1. Edit a manifest under k8s/ in your fork — the GitLab Web IDE or a local clone.
  2. Commit and push to main on your fork.
  3. Argo CD auto-syncs within the reconcile interval; the Refresh button in the Argo CD UI (http://localhost:30002) forces it instantly.

Do not kubectl apply into the casino namespace

Argo CD selfHeal reverts any hand-drift. Your GitLab fork is the single source of truth — if a change is not committed there, it does not persist.

docs.title: The agent loop: Problem → Opencode → Verify
docs.text:
Every step from here on follows one canonical pattern. You never hand-author the fix from a blank file — you observe the symptom in Dynatrace, then drive the opencode coding agent (warmed up in Step 0) to produce it, review the diff, apply it, and verify with a DQL checkpoint. Learn the loop once here; every step is a variation on it.

flowchart LR p["① Problemsee the symptom in Dynatrace(missing span, climbing series, PII)"] o["② Opencodeprompt the agent: goal + target file + skill"] r["③ Reviewread the diff it produces"] a["④ Applyapp → commit → Argo synccollector → kubectl apply"] v["⑤ Verifyre-run the DQL checkpoint"] p --> o --> r --> a --> v v -. "not fixed? steer it back" .-> o

Each step gives you a copy-pasteable prompt with three things the agent needs:

  1. The goal — what telemetry should exist afterwards, in plain terms.
  2. The target file — e.g. observability/collectors/gateway.yaml for a collector fix, or the slots service source for an instrumentation fix.
  3. The skill — which installed Agent Skill to lean on: otel-instrumentation for SDK code, otel-collector / otel-ottl for pipeline and transform logic, otel-semantic-conventions for the Weaver registry, dt-* for Dynatrace/DQL.

When the agent gets it wrong — steer it back, don't hand-fix

opencode is not deterministic. If the diff misses an attribute, puts a processor in the wrong pipeline order, or invents a field name, reply with the specific correction rather than editing by hand — e.g. "memory_limiter must stay the first processor and batch the last; move your new processor between k8sattributes and batch." Steering the agent is the skill this track teaches; the verify checkpoint tells you when you are done.

Apply differs by target. App-code fixes (Steps 1–2) go through Git — commit → push → Argo CD sync — because the casino namespace is GitOps-owned (selfHeal reverts hand-drift). Collector fixes (Steps 4–7) are applied with kubectl apply against the observability namespace, which Argo does not manage.

docs.title: The collector is the control point
docs.text:
Steps 4–7 all change one collector — the gateway — never the apps. That is deliberate: a gateway change covers traces, metrics, and logs for the whole cluster at once. The pipelines obey three invariants that never change, no matter which processor you add:

flowchart LR otlp["OTLP in(gRPC/HTTP)"] --> ml["memory_limiter(always first)"] ml --> k8s["k8sattributes(Kubernetes enrichment)"] k8s --> mid["step 4–7 processorscost / cardinality / PII / sampling"] mid --> batch["batch(always last)"] batch --> dtx["otlphttp → Dynatrace"]

The three invariants

  • memory_limiter is always the first processor.
  • batch is always the last processor.
  • k8sattributes does the Kubernetes enrichment (we run in Kubernetes — we never use resourcedetection here).

The known-good baseline is observability/collectors/gateway.yaml in the repo. The fully composed end-state — steps 4+5+6+7 wired in the correct order — is labs/advanced/gateway-advanced.yaml.

docs.title: Dynatrace validation checkpoint
docs.text:
Confirm the environment is live and see the planted issues you will fix:

  1. Infrastructure → Kubernetes — your cluster (by PARTICIPANT_ID) is present.
  2. Distributed traces — a trickle of casino traces is already flowing (k6 is playing for you). The casino's money-path (the actual spin/payout) is not visible yet — that is Step 1's job.
  3. Logs — casino log lines are arriving with player PII intact (Step 6).
  4. Metrics / Account Management → Cost allocation — telemetry sits in one undifferentiated cost bucket, and at least one metric's series count is climbing (Steps 4 and 5). The money-path has traces but no business metrics yet — no bet count, no wager histogram (Step 2).

Argo CD should show the casino Application Synced / Healthy:

kubectl -n argocd get application casino
kubectl -n argocd get secret casino-repo -o jsonpath='{.data.url}' | base64 -d; echo
# -> https://<gitlab-host>/<attendee>/casino.git

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• You can name each component and its namespace
  • casino Application shows Synced / Healthy in Argo CD
  • The casino-repo secret points at your GitLab fork
  • You can state the three collector-pipeline invariants
  • You have seen the planted issues in Dynatrace (missing money-path, PII in logs, single cost bucket, climbing cardinality)

Next: Step 0 — Warmup.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Goal: have the tokens you need, a fork of the casino project on the Dynatrace-solution GitLab, and a Codespace starting against that fork. Budget 15 minutes.

This is the advanced self-paced track

These pages sit alongside the facilitator-led modules M0–M5, not in place of them. Where M0–M5 walk one planted defect at a time with a helper in the room, this track is a self-paced sequence of seven larger exercises (plus a Step 0 warmup) — instrumentation, business metrics, a semantic-convention guard, cost, cardinality, PII, and sampling. Every step follows one pattern — the Problem → Opencode → Verify loop, where you drive the opencode AI coding agent to produce each fix — and ends with a Dynatrace validation checkpoint you run yourself.

docs.title: 1. Tokens you need
docs.text:
Everyone shares one Dynatrace tenant; your work is kept separate by your k8s.cluster.name. Before you create the Codespace, make sure you have the following. The three Dynatrace values are injected as Codespace secrets by the organizers — you usually do not mint them yourself, but you should know what they are and how to check them.

For the authoritative type/consumer of every Dynatrace variable, see the one canonical table in M0 setup → Environment variables. The subset you need for this track:

Secret What it is Dynatrace docs DT_TENANT Your tenant URL, e.g. https://abc12345.live.dynatrace.com Environment / tenant DT_INGEST_TOKEN Platform token (dt0s16) — OTLP ingest, scopes openpipeline:{traces,metrics,logs,events}:ingest + storage:metrics:write Platform tokens DT_OPERATOR_TOKEN Platform token (dt0s16) for Kubernetes monitoring (ActiveGate / operator) — fleet-management:* + settings:objects:*. Renamed from DT_API_TOKEN, still accepted as a deprecated fallback. Platform tokens DT_PLATFORM_TOKEN (optional) Platform token (dt0s16) used only by dtctl — same token type as the two above but a distinct scope set Platform tokens GITLAB_REPO_URL HTTPS URL of your casino fork (see step 2) — GITLAB_TOKEN Token scoped to your fork (read_repository + write_repository) GitLab access tokens WORKSHOP_DISPENSER_URL Endpoint that mints your per-attendee LLM proxy key (for opencode in Step 1) — not a Dynatrace token — WORKSHOP_ROOM_PASSWORD Shared room password sent to the dispenser — not a Dynatrace token —

The two WORKSHOP_* secrets are only for Step 1

They wire the opencode AI coding agent to a facilitator-hosted LLM proxy. If they are not set, the Codespace still comes up fully — only the Step 1 AI-agent instrumentation flow is unavailable (post-create setup says so and moves on). Your per-attendee budget is enforced on the proxy; there is nothing to configure for it locally.

Davis CoPilot (optional) — a separate OAuth client

If your cohort runs the optional Davis CoPilot exercise, it uses a Dynatrace OAuth client (dt0s02), not any of the tokens above. It is kept deliberately separate from the required DT token set and is only wired when that exercise is in scope. Nothing on the main M0–M5 path or in this track's required steps needs it, so skip it unless a facilitator says otherwise.

You never paste a token into the repo

Tokens live only as Codespace secrets and are read at runtime. Nothing is written to disk or committed. If you ever find yourself pasting a token into a file, stop — that is not the flow.

docs.title: 2. Fork the casino project (do this before the Codespace)
docs.text:
This track uses GitLab + Argo CD, because GitLab is part of the Dynatrace solution. You fork the upstream casino project into the shared GitLab, and your Codespace's Argo CD syncs from your fork.

Placeholders below: <gitlab-host> is the Dynatrace-solution GitLab from your welcome email; <attendee> is your GitLab username.

  1. Sign in to the shared GitLab at https://<gitlab-host>/ with the account from your welcome email.
  2. Open the upstream project https://<gitlab-host>/otel-training/casino.
  3. Click Fork and select your namespace. You now own https://<gitlab-host>/<attendee>/casino, containing the Kubernetes manifests under k8s/.

docs.title: Create a token scoped to your fork
docs.text:
1. In your fork → Settings → Access Tokens (a Project Access Token), or your user Preferences → Access Tokens (a Personal Access Token).
  2. Scopes: read_repository (Argo CD pulls from the fork) and write_repository (so you can push your edits back).
  3. Copy the token value now — GitLab will not show it again.

docs.title: 3. Inject the fork URL and token as Codespace secrets
docs.text:
In GitHub → Settings → Codespaces → Repository secrets (or at Codespace creation time), set:

Secret Value GITLAB_REPO_URL https://<gitlab-host>/<attendee>/casino.git GITLAB_TOKEN the token from step 2 GITLAB_USERNAME (optional) your username; defaults to oauth2, which is valid for GitLab tokens over HTTPS

docs.title: 4. Start the Codespace
docs.text:
1. Open the training repository you received in your welcome email.
  2. Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main.
  3. Post-create setup runs automatically. Seeing GITOPS_PROVIDER=gitlab plus your two GitLab secrets, it installs Argo CD and points the casino Application at your fork. Typically 3–5 minutes with a prebuild.

Offline / air-gapped fallback

If the GitLab secrets are not present, the bootstrap falls back to an in-cluster Gitea host (GITOPS_PROVIDER=gitea) and prints how to switch. The Argo CD lab loop is identical either way — only the Git host differs.

docs.title: Dynatrace validation checkpoint
docs.text:
You have not instrumented anything yet, so this checkpoint just proves the plumbing:

  1. echo $DT_TENANT, open the URL, and sign in with the credentials from your handout.
  2. Go to Infrastructure → Kubernetes and confirm a cluster named after your PARTICIPANT_ID appears (first appearance can take a few minutes).
  3. Set a filter k8s.cluster.name = your PARTICIPANT_ID and save the view. You will reuse it on every step.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• You can name the secrets in the table above and what each is for
  • You own a fork https://<gitlab-host>/<attendee>/casino
  • GITLAB_REPO_URL and GITLAB_TOKEN are set as Codespace secrets
  • The Codespace is created on main and post-create setup finished
  • Your cluster appears under Infrastructure → Kubernetes in Dynatrace

Next: The environment.

docs.title: Step 0 — Warmup
docs.text:
Goal: get your AI coding agent ready before you touch any telemetry. By the end of this page opencode is open, authenticated to the workshop LLM proxy, and has all three skill sets loaded — Dynatrace (dt-*), OpenTelemetry (otel-*), and the dtctl CLI skill. You will prove each one with a safe, read-only task, then run your first real agent task: asking the agent to explain the gateway pipeline you just met in The environment. Budget 15 minutes.

Every later step drives opencode through the Problem → Opencode → Verify loop. This page is where you make sure the agent actually works, so a failure on Step 1 is a telemetry problem, never a tooling problem.

docs.title: 1. Open opencode and confirm it answers
docs.text:
opencode is baked into the Codespace image and wired at start-up to the facilitator-hosted LLM proxy (the two WORKSHOP_* secrets from Getting started). It starts in build mode, so it can read and edit files in your working tree directly. Confirm it is alive:

opencode --version
opencode run "reply with the single word READY"   # returns a model completion

If that last command hangs or errors, the proxy key was not minted — jump to Troubleshooting → Workshop LLM proxy before going further. Nothing else on this track works until opencode run returns a completion.

docs.title: 2. Confirm the skills loaded
docs.text:
Agent Skills are what let opencode reason correctly about Dynatrace and OpenTelemetry instead of guessing. The bootstrap installs three sets into ~/.config/opencode/skills/. Confirm they are present with the lab-readiness gate and the raw list the agent sees:

bash .devcontainer/bootstrap/verify-opencode-skills.sh   # exit 0 = opencode + all three sets loadable
opencode debug skill                                     # the raw skill list opencode has

You are looking for three families in that list:

Family Prefix What it gives the agent Dynatrace-for-AI dt-* DQL syntax, observability patterns, Kubernetes/cloud topology (38 skills) OpenTelemetry otel-* otel-instrumentation, otel-ottl, otel-dynatrace (+ otel-collector / otel-semantic-conventions as upstream ships them) dtctl dtctl Driving the dtctl CLI to read and apply Dynatrace config

If a family is missing — install it, don't skip it

The skill install is non-fatal at bootstrap, so a GitHub blip can leave a set out. Re-run the installer (it is idempotent):

bash .devcontainer/bootstrap/install-opencode-skills.sh

On a machine with Node you can add the OpenTelemetry set directly instead:

npx skills add henrikrexed/observability-agent-skills@v1.0.0

Both land in ~/.config/opencode/skills/. Re-run verify-opencode-skills.sh until it exits 0 before you continue.

docs.title: 3. Test the dtctl skill — a safe read-only task
docs.text:
Before you let the agent change anything, prove it can read Dynatrace through the dtctl skill. This is read-only — it lists config, it does not apply:

opencode run "Using the dtctl skill, list the Dynatrace environment dtctl is \
pointed at and show me one read-only command to list existing dashboards. Do \
not apply anything."

A good answer names your DT_TENANT and proposes something like dtctl get dashboards (or the skill's documented read verb) without running any mutating command. If the agent tries to apply or delete, steer it back: "read-only only — just show me the command, do not run a mutation." That corrective reply is the exact muscle you will use on every later step.

docs.title: 4. Install / confirm the OpenTelemetry skills
docs.text:
Step 1 onward leans on the otel-* skills. If step 2's table already showed otel-instrumentation, otel-ottl, and otel-dynatrace, you are done — skip ahead. If not, install them now with the same command from the warning above and re-verify:

bash .devcontainer/bootstrap/install-opencode-skills.sh
opencode debug skill | grep otel-

You should see at least otel-instrumentation, otel-ottl, and otel-dynatrace.

docs.title: 5. Your first real agent task — explain the gateway pipeline
docs.text:
Now use the agent to understand, not change, the pipeline from The environment. This warms up the otel-collector reasoning and confirms the agent can read repo files:

opencode run "Read observability/collectors/gateway.yaml and explain, in order, \
every processor in the traces pipeline. For each, say what it does and why its \
position matters. Confirm memory_limiter is first and batch is last, and tell me \
where a NEW processor would have to go to respect those two invariants."

A correct answer walks the processors top-to-bottom, states that memory_limiter is first and batch is last, and says a new processor belongs between k8sattributes and batch. That is the invariant you will enforce by hand every time you steer the agent on Steps 4–7 — now you have seen the agent state it itself.

If the agent hallucinates the file

If opencode describes a pipeline that is not in the file (wrong exporter, invented processor), reply "only describe what is actually in observability/collectors/gateway.yaml — quote the processors array." Grounding the agent in the real file is a habit worth building before Step 1.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• opencode run "reply with READY" returns a completion (proxy is wired)
  • verify-opencode-skills.sh exits 0
  • opencode debug skill lists dt-*, otel-*, and dtctl
  • The agent produced a read-only dtctl command (and you steered it if it didn't)
  • The agent correctly explained the gateway pipeline order and the memory_limiter-first / batch-last invariants

Next: Step 1 — Instrument with AI agents.

docs.title: Step 1 — Instrument with AI agents
docs.text: Goal: make the casino's money-path observable. Auto-instrumentation gives you the HTTP and DB edges for free, but the business logic — the bet, the RNG draw, the payout decision — is a black box. You will run the Problem → Opencode → Verify loop from The environment for the first time: see the missing money-path in Dynatrace, drive opencode (warmed up in Step 0) with the otel-instrumentation skill to add manual spans and domain attributes, review the diff, commit for Argo CD to redeploy, and confirm the span shows up. Budget 30 minutes.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
flowchart TB subgraph before["Before — auto-instrumentation only"] b1["POST /spin"] --> b2["duration onlyno game, bet, outcome, payout"] end subgraph after["After — manual span added"] a1["POST /spin"] --> a2["casino.slots.spingame · bet · outcome · payout"] end

Auto-instrumentation shows a generic POST /spin server span with a duration, but nothing about which game, the bet size, the outcome, or the payout. So you cannot answer "are high-value bets losing more often?" or "which game drives payout cost?". You add a child span that carries the domain.

docs.title: ① Problem — the planted gap
docs.text:
The slots service (vegas-slots-service, Node.js) ships deliberately under-instrumented. It wires only the auto-instrumentation SDK, so its /spin handler computes outcome and payout with no manual span and no domain attributes. In Dynatrace the symptom is stark: a spin is a featureless POST /spin server span — flat duration, and because the business logic runs inside that one handler with no child span, the money-path shows up as an orphaned, undifferentiated operation with nothing you can slice by. Reference asset (the planted state): labs/advanced/step1-agent-instrumentation/before.slots-index.js.

Planted gaps you will see and fix:

  • No child span around the outcome/payout computation — the variable, interesting part of the request is invisible inside the generic server span.
  • No casino.* domain attributes — you cannot answer "are high-value bets losing more often?" or "which game drives payout cost?".
  • Losing-edge errors are swallowed — a settlement failure throws with no span event and no error status, so it never surfaces in trace analysis.

Confirm the symptom first — run the checkpoint DQL at the foot of this page now and watch it return zero rows. That is your "before".

docs.title: ② Opencode — drive the fix
docs.text:
You already proved opencode and its skills work in Step 0. Now use it for real. Clone your casino fork, cd into it, and drive the agent at the slots service source with the otel-instrumentation skill — the prompt names the goal, the target file, and the skill:

opencode run "Using the otel-instrumentation skill: in the vegas-slots-service \
/spin handler, wrap the draw and payout in a child span 'casino.slots.spin' with \
@opentelemetry/api. Set attributes casino.game.name, casino.bet.amount, \
casino.outcome, casino.payout.amount; add a 'jackpot' span event on a jackpot; \
set span error status on failures. Keep the existing response shape."

docs.title: ③ Review — read the diff
docs.text:
In build mode opencode writes the change straight into the working tree. Read the diff before you commit. The target shape the agent should converge on (from after.slots-index.js):

+ const { trace, SpanStatusCode } = require('@opentelemetry/api');
+ const tracer = trace.getTracer('casino-slots', '1.0.0');
  app.post('/spin', async (req, res) => {
-   const bet = Number(req.body.bet);
-   const outcome = draw();
-   const payout = settle(bet, outcome);
-   res.json({ outcome, payout });
+   const bet = Number(req.body.bet);
+   await tracer.startActiveSpan('casino.slots.spin', async (span) => {
+     try {
+       span.setAttribute('casino.game.name', 'slots');
+       span.setAttribute('casino.bet.amount', bet);
+       const outcome = draw();
+       const payout = settle(bet, outcome);
+       span.setAttribute('casino.outcome', outcome.kind);        // win | lose | jackpot
+       span.setAttribute('casino.payout.amount', payout);
+       if (outcome.kind === 'jackpot') span.addEvent('jackpot', { 'casino.payout.amount': payout });
+       res.json({ outcome, payout });
+     } catch (err) {
+       span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR, message: err.message });
+       span.recordException(err);
+       throw err;
+     } finally {
+       span.end();
+     }
+   });
  });

Why these exact attribute names?

casino.game.name, casino.bet.amount, casino.outcome, casino.payout.amount. Step 1 creates these attributes; Step 3 (Weaver) guards them, and Step 2 reuses casino.game.name / casino.outcome as the dimensions on the business metrics. Keep the names exactly as above or the Step 3 registry check will flag drift.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

Common misses and the one-line correction to reply with:

  • Attribute dropped or renamed (casino.game instead of casino.game.name): "use exactly these four keys, dotted: casino.game.name, casino.bet.amount, casino.outcome, casino.payout.amount."
  • No error path: "wrap the body in try/catch and set SpanStatusCode.ERROR + recordException on failure."
  • Response shape changed: "keep the existing res.json({ outcome, payout }) response untouched."

Re-run opencode with the correction rather than hand-editing — the verify checkpoint tells you when the agent is done.

The same pattern applies to roulette/dice/blackjack. The Java scoring service runs under the OTel Java agent (zero-code), so there you add @WithSpan("casino.scoring.settleRound") and @SpanAttribute annotations (opentelemetry-instrumentation-annotations) rather than hand-building the span:

@WithSpan("casino.scoring.settleRound")
public Payout settleRound(@SpanAttribute("casino.game.name") String game,
                          @SpanAttribute("casino.bet.amount") long bet) {
    // ... scoring logic ...
}

docs.title: ④ Apply — commit → Argo CD sync
docs.text:
The casino namespace is GitOps-owned, so you apply app-code fixes through Git, not kubectl:

git add . && git commit -m "feat(slots): add casino.slots.spin money-path span"
git push            # to your fork's main

Argo CD syncs within the reconcile interval (hit Refresh in the UI at http://localhost:30002 to force it), redeploys the slots service, then play a few rounds of slots to generate traffic.

docs.title: ⑤ Verify — Dynatrace validation checkpoint
docs.text:
Run in a Grail Notebook against the training tenant (filter to your cluster):

fetch spans
| filter span.name == "casino.slots.spin"
| summarize spins = count(), avgPayout = avg(toDouble(casino.payout.amount)) by { casino.outcome }
  • Before: the query returns no rows — the span does not exist, the money-path is invisible.
  • After: one row per casino.outcome (win / lose / jackpot) with payout aggregates, and the casino.slots.spin span appears as a child of POST /spin in the distributed trace.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• casino.slots.spin child span wraps the draw+payout
  • It carries casino.game.name, casino.bet.amount, casino.outcome, casino.payout.amount
  • The jackpot path records a span event; errors set span status
  • The DQL returns one row per outcome with payout aggregates
  • The span is a child of POST /spin in the trace flow

Next: Step 2 — Business metrics.

docs.title: Step 2 — Business metrics
docs.text: Goal: turn the money-path you instrumented in Step 1 into business metrics you can chart and alert on. Traces answer "what happened on this one spin"; metrics answer "how many bets, and how much wagered, by game and outcome, over time". You will run the Problem → Opencode → Verify loop again — this time adding a counter (casino.bets.count) and a histogram (casino.wager.amount) to the slots service with the otel-instrumentation skill — then build a DQL tile. Budget 25 minutes.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
flowchart TB subgraph before["Before — traces only"] b1["casino.slots.spin span"] --> b2["per-spin detailbut no aggregate volume/value"] end subgraph after["After — business metrics added"] a1["casino.bets.count (counter)"] --> a2["bets per game × outcome"] a3["casino.wager.amount (histogram)"] --> a4["wager distribution:p50 / p90 / max by game"] end

A span is a per-event record — great for "show me this trace", expensive to aggregate over millions of rows. A metric is pre-aggregated and cheap to query over long windows, so it is what a dashboard or SLO reads. The casino money-path has rich spans after Step 1 but no first-class business metrics: there is no cheap way to chart "bets per minute on slots" or "wager-size distribution by outcome". You add two instruments:

Instrument Name Why this type Counter casino.bets.count Monotonic event count — bets placed, by game and outcome. Rolls up to a rate. Histogram casino.wager.amount A distribution — you want p50/p90/max wager, not just a sum, so a histogram (not a counter) is the right instrument.

Both carry the same dimensions as the Step 1 span — casino.game.name and casino.outcome — so the metric and the trace share one vocabulary (and the Step 3 Weaver registry can guard both).

Bounded dimensions only — on purpose

Dimension the metrics only by casino.game.name (4 values) and casino.outcome (3 values) — never by player.id or round.id. That is the same cardinality discipline you enforce at the gateway in Step 5; here you simply never emit the unbounded labels in the first place.

docs.title: ① Problem — no business metrics on the money-path
docs.text:
After Step 1 the slots service emits a casino.slots.spin span per request, but the /spin handler never records a metric. Reference asset (the planted state): labs/advanced/step-business-metrics/before.slots-metrics.js.

Confirm the symptom — run the checkpoint DQL for casino.bets.count now and watch it return no such metric. That is your "before": you can pull individual spins, but you cannot cheaply chart bet volume or wager distribution.

docs.title: ② Opencode — add the counter and histogram
docs.text:
Drive opencode at the slots service with the otel-instrumentation skill. The prompt names the goal, the target file, and the skill:

opencode run "Using the otel-instrumentation skill: in the vegas-slots-service \
/spin handler, add OpenTelemetry metrics via @opentelemetry/api metrics. Create \
a Counter 'casino.bets.count' and a Histogram 'casino.wager.amount' (unit chips) \
from a meter 'casino-slots'. On each settled spin, add 1 to the counter and \
record the bet amount to the histogram, both with attributes casino.game.name \
and casino.outcome — matching the Step 1 span. Do NOT add player.id or round.id. \
Keep the existing span and response shape."

docs.title: ③ Review — read the diff
docs.text:
Read the diff before committing. The target shape (from labs/advanced/step-business-metrics/after.slots-metrics.js):

+ const { metrics } = require('@opentelemetry/api');
+ const meter = metrics.getMeter('casino-slots', '1.0.0');
+ const betsCount = meter.createCounter('casino.bets.count', {
+   description: 'Number of bets placed', unit: '{bet}',
+ });
+ const wagerAmount = meter.createHistogram('casino.wager.amount', {
+   description: 'Distribution of wagered amounts', unit: '{chip}',
+ });
  app.post('/spin', async (req, res) => {
    const bet = Number(req.body.bet);
    await tracer.startActiveSpan('casino.slots.spin', async (span) => {
      // ... existing span attributes from Step 1 ...
      const outcome = draw();
      const payout = settle(bet, outcome);
      span.setAttribute('casino.outcome', outcome.kind);
      span.setAttribute('casino.payout.amount', payout);
+     const dims = { 'casino.game.name': 'slots', 'casino.outcome': outcome.kind };
+     betsCount.add(1, dims);
+     wagerAmount.record(bet, dims);
      res.json({ outcome, payout });
      // ... existing error handling + span.end() ...
    });
  });

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

  • Uses a counter for the wager (casino.wager.amount as a Counter): "wager.amount must be a Histogram — I want p50/p90, not a running sum."
  • Adds high-cardinality dims (player.id, round.id): "only casino.game.name and casino.outcome as dimensions — drop any per-player or per-round label."
  • Creates a new meter per request (inside the handler): "create the meter and instruments once at module scope, not inside the /spin handler."

docs.title: ④ Apply — commit → Argo CD sync
docs.text:
Same GitOps apply as Step 1 — the slots service is in the casino namespace:

git add . && git commit -m "feat(slots): add casino.bets.count + casino.wager.amount metrics"
git push            # to your fork's main

Argo CD redeploys the service (hit Refresh at http://localhost:30002 to force the sync); play a few rounds of slots so the instruments emit.

docs.title: Dynatrace validation checkpoint
docs.text:
Run in a Grail Notebook against the training tenant (filter to your cluster).

Bet volume by game and outcome (the counter, as a rate):

timeseries bets = sum(casino.bets.count), by: { casino.game.name, casino.outcome }, from: now() - 1h

Wager-size distribution (the histogram — p50/p90/max):

timeseries wager_p90 = percentile(casino.wager.amount, 90), by: { casino.game.name }, from: now() - 1h
  • Before: both metrics are absent — casino.bets.count / casino.wager.amount do not exist; the queries return nothing.
  • After: casino.bets.count returns one series per casino.game.name × casino.outcome (≤ 12 series — bounded on purpose), and casino.wager.amount returns a p90 wager per game.

docs.title: Build a DQL tile
docs.text:
Pin the first query as a tile so you have a live "bets per minute by outcome" chart — this is the business view a casino operator would actually watch:

  1. In the Notebook, run the casino.bets.count query above.
  2. Switch the visualization to a line chart, split by casino.outcome.
  3. Add to dashboard → a dashboard named after your PARTICIPANT_ID.

Why a histogram for wager, a counter for bets

A counter answers how many (and its rate). A histogram answers what distribution — the p90 wager is what tells you whether a few whales or many small bets drive volume. Picking the instrument type to match the question is the core skill here; the agent will follow whichever you specify, so specify deliberately.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• casino.bets.count counter and casino.wager.amount histogram emitted from the slots service
  • Both carry only casino.game.name + casino.outcome (no player/round id)
  • The counter DQL returns ≤ 12 bounded series
  • The histogram DQL returns a p90 wager per game
  • A "bets by outcome" tile is pinned to your dashboard

Next: Step 3 — Weaver pipeline.

docs.title: Step 3 — Weaver pipeline
docs.text:
The labs/advanced/ directories keep their original feature-ordinal numbering, so they run one behind these doc steps — this page's assets live under labs/advanced/step2-weaver-semconv/.

Optional / stretch step

Weaver is a build-time governance guard, not a telemetry fix. If you are tight on time, skim the concept and move to Step 4 — the money-path is already observable after Steps 1–2. Come back here when you want to stop those attributes from rotting.

Goal: stop the attributes you created in Step 1 (and reused for the Step 2 metrics) from silently rotting. You will turn the casino.* conventions into a versioned registry and a CI check that fails the pull request on drift. Budget 25 minutes.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Step 1 introduced casino.* attributes by hand. Without a guard, the next refactor renames casino.bet.amount → casino.betAmount, or adds a round.id dimension to a metric, and every dashboard, DQL query, and alert that depends on the old name breaks — silently. Weaver makes the conventions a versioned registry and a CI check.

flowchart LR pr["Pull requestrenames casino.bet.amount"] --> ci["CI: weaver registry check"] ci -->|conventions intact| green["exit 0 — merge allowed"] ci -->|drift detected| red["exit non-zero — merge blocked"] red -.->|protects| dt["Dynatrace contentstays valid"]

docs.title: The assets
docs.text:
From labs/advanced/step2-weaver-semconv/:

registry/
  registry_manifest.yaml     # registry name + version
  models/casino.yaml         # the casino.* attribute registry + span & metric conventions
weaver-policies/
  casino_policies.rego       # extra guards: snake_case naming + no high-card metric dims
ci/weaver-check.yml          # GitHub Actions workflow running `weaver registry check`

docs.title: Before — no guard
docs.text: No registry, no CI check. A rename or a stray high-cardinality dimension merges freely and Dynatrace content silently rots. This is the status quo you start from.

docs.title: ② Opencode — add the guard
docs.text:
Unlike the collector steps, the fix here is a registry, not a pipeline change. Drive opencode with the otel-semantic-conventions skill to author (or extend) the registry from the casino.* attributes already in the code — goal, target dir, skill:

opencode run "Using the otel-semantic-conventions skill: review the casino.* \
attributes and metrics used in the slots service, and make \
labs/advanced/step2-weaver-semconv/registry a complete Weaver registry covering \
casino.game.name, casino.bet.amount, casino.outcome, casino.payout.amount and \
the Step 2 metrics casino.bets.count / casino.wager.amount. Enforce snake/dotted \
naming and forbid high-cardinality metric dimensions in the rego policy."

Review the diff, then run the same command CI runs (exit 0 means conventions intact):

weaver registry check \
  --registry labs/advanced/step2-weaver-semconv/registry \
  --policy   labs/advanced/step2-weaver-semconv/weaver-policies

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

If the agent invents attributes the code does not emit, reply "only include casino. keys that actually appear in the slots service source and the Step 2 metrics — quote each one."* The committed registry/models/casino.yaml is the reference answer.

docs.title: Watch the guard fire
docs.text:
Introduce drift and confirm it is blocked:

# camelCase drift → policy deny
sed -i 's/casino.bet.amount/casino.betAmount/' registry/models/casino.yaml
weaver registry check --registry registry --policy weaver-policies
#  → FAIL: casino attribute 'casino.betAmount' must be snake_case (no camelCase)

A high-cardinality dimension on the payout metric (adding - ref: casino.round.id under metric.casino.payout) is denied the same way. Revert the edit and the check goes green again.

The CI job gates merges

In the casino repo the weaver-semconv-check job runs on services/** changes, so drift can never reach main. Weaver is pinned in ci/weaver-check.yml.

docs.title: Dynatrace validation checkpoint
docs.text:
Weaver is a build-time guard, so its primary checkpoint is CI: green vs red. The downstream Dynatrace evidence: because the names are stable, the Step 1 DQL keeps returning rows across releases.

fetch spans
| filter span.name == "casino.slots.spin"
| summarize spins = count() by { casino.outcome }
  • With the guard: rows keep coming after every release — the attribute names never silently change.
  • Contrast (a "renamed attribute" branch with no guard): the same DQL returns zero rows — exactly the regression Weaver would have blocked.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• weaver registry check exits 0 on the intact registry
  • A camelCase rename is denied by policy
  • A high-cardinality metric dimension is denied by policy
  • The weaver-semconv-check CI job is wired for services/**
  • The Step 1 DQL still returns rows (names held stable)

Next: Step 4 — Cost of observability.

docs.title: Step 4 — Cost of observability
docs.text:
The labs/advanced/ directories keep their original feature-ordinal numbering, so they run one behind these doc steps — this page's assets live under labs/advanced/step3-cost-center/.

Goal: attribute your telemetry spend. You cannot manage what you cannot attribute, so you will inject the Dynatrace cost-center attributes at the gateway and read ingest split per cost center. Budget 20 minutes.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Dynatrace Cost Allocation reads two resource attributes — dt.cost.costcenter and dt.cost.product. Once every signal carries them, DDU consumption can be split per team/product and charged back. Injecting at the gateway (not per app) means one change covers traces, metrics, and logs for the whole cluster.

flowchart LR casino["casino services"] -->|OTLP| gw["gateway collector"] gw --> rc["resource/costcentersets dt.cost.costcenter + dt.cost.product"] rc --> dt[("DynatraceCost allocation")] dt --> split["DDU split percost center / product"]

docs.title: Before — one undifferentiated bucket
docs.text: The baseline gateway exports telemetry with no dt.cost.* attributes, so Account Management → Cost allocation shows everything under a single bucket. You cannot answer "how much does the casino platform cost vs the scoring service?".

docs.title: ② Opencode — inject the cost-center at the gateway
docs.text:
This is the first collector fix, so you drive opencode at the gateway config with the otel-collector skill — goal, target file, skill:

opencode run "Using the otel-collector skill: in observability/collectors/gateway.yaml \
add a resource processor named resource/costcenter that sets the resource \
attributes dt.cost.costcenter and dt.cost.product from the env vars COST_CENTER \
and COST_PRODUCT. Wire it into all three pipelines AFTER k8sattributes and BEFORE \
batch. Do not move memory_limiter (first) or batch (last)."

docs.title: ③ Review — read the diff
docs.text:
Confirm the processor lands after k8sattributes, before batch in every pipeline and that memory_limiter stays first. The reference answer is labs/advanced/step3-cost-center/cost-center-processor.yaml, already merged into the composed labs/advanced/gateway-advanced.yaml in the correct position.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

If it puts the processor before k8sattributes or after batch, reply "memory_limiter must stay first and batch last; a resource processor goes between k8sattributes and batch — move it there in every pipeline."

docs.title: ④ Apply — kubectl (collector namespace, not GitOps)
docs.text:
The gateway lives in the observability namespace, which Argo CD does not manage, so you apply it directly:

# set the cost center for your team, then apply the edited gateway
kubectl -n observability set env deployment/otel-gateway-collector \
  COST_CENTER=casino-platform-training COST_PRODUCT=vegas-casino
kubectl apply -f observability/collectors/gateway.yaml

Every span, metric, and log the gateway exports now carries dt.cost.costcenter=casino-platform-training and dt.cost.product=vegas-casino.

Why resource-level, and why at the gateway

dt.cost.* are resource attributes — they describe the source, not a single event, so the resource processor is the right tool. Putting it at the gateway means you tag all three signals in one place instead of touching every service SDK.

docs.title: Dynatrace validation checkpoint
docs.text:
Cost/ingest readout — volume split by cost center over the last hour, in a Grail Notebook:

fetch logs, from: now() - 1h
| filter isNotNull(dt.cost.costcenter)
| summarize ingested = count() by { dt.cost.costcenter, dt.cost.product }
| sort ingested desc
  • Before: dt.cost.costcenter is null everywhere → a single undifferentiated bucket.
  • After: one row per cost center/product; Account Management → Cost allocation attributes DDU consumption to casino-platform-training.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• The resource/costcenter processor is wired into the gateway (after k8sattributes, before batch)
  • COST_CENTER / COST_PRODUCT are set on the gateway deployment
  • The DQL returns rows keyed by dt.cost.costcenter / dt.cost.product
  • Cost allocation in Dynatrace splits DDU per cost center

Next: Step 5 — High-cardinality metrics.

docs.title: Step 5 — High-cardinality metrics
docs.text:
The labs/advanced/ directories keep their original feature-ordinal numbering, so they run one behind these doc steps — this page's assets live under labs/advanced/step4-high-cardinality/.

Goal: find a metric whose cost is exploding, understand why, and fix it at the collector without an app redeploy. Budget 25 minutes.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Metrics are cheap per series and ruinous per unbounded dimension. One round.id label turns a 12-series counter into millions of series. You find the offender in Dynatrace, then strip the offending dimensions at the gateway.

flowchart LR before["casino.payout.total+ round.id + player.id"] -->|"series = millions"| warn["cardinality warningchart unusable"] before --> fix["transform/cardinalitystrip round.id, player.id"] fix --> after["casino.payout.totalgame.name × outcome"] after -->|"series ≈ 12"| ok["chart renders instantly"]

docs.title: Before — the offending metric
docs.text: casino.payout.total carries round.id and player.id (see labs/advanced/step4-high-cardinality/before.offending-metric.md). Every distinct round and player is a new series, so the series count grows without bound.

docs.title: ② Opencode — strip the dimensions at the gateway
docs.text:
Drive opencode at the gateway with the otel-ottl skill — stripping metric labels is an OTTL transform, so name that skill explicitly:

opencode run "Using the otel-ottl and otel-collector skills: in \
observability/collectors/gateway.yaml add a transform/cardinality processor that \
deletes the metric datapoint attributes round.id and player.id (OTTL: \
delete_key(attributes, \"round.id\")). Wire it into the metrics pipeline only, \
after k8sattributes and before batch. Leave memory_limiter first and batch last."

docs.title: ③ Review — read the diff
docs.text:
Confirm it uses OTTL delete_key on the two offending attributes, sits in the metrics pipeline (not traces/logs), and respects first/last. Reference answer: labs/advanced/step4-high-cardinality/cardinality-fix-processor.yaml.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

If it strips the wrong keys or adds the processor to every pipeline, reply "only the metrics pipeline, and only delete round.id and player.id — keep casino.game.name and casino.outcome."

docs.title: ④ Apply — kubectl
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f observability/collectors/gateway.yaml

The gateway strips round.id / player.id and the counter collapses back to casino.game.name × casino.outcome (≤ 12 series).

You did not lose the per-round view

Per-round drill-down still exists — on the spans from Step 1, where cardinality is free. Metrics answer "how much, by bounded dimension"; traces answer "what happened on this specific round". Use each for what it is cheap at.

docs.title: Dynatrace validation checkpoint
docs.text:
Cardinality readout — distinct series on the metric over the last hour, in a Grail Notebook:

timeseries cnt = count(), by: { casino.game.name, casino.outcome }, from: now() - 1h
| fieldsAdd metric = "casino.payout.total"
| summarize series = count()

Or inspect the dimension cardinality directly in Metrics → casino.payout.total → Dimensions.

  • Before: the dimension count climbs continuously (thousands → millions); the chart is unusable and a cardinality warning appears.
  • After: a flat ~12 series (4 games × 3 outcomes); the chart renders instantly and ingest cost drops.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• You identified round.id / player.id as the offending dimensions
  • The transform/cardinality processor is wired into the metrics pipeline
  • The series count is flat at ~12 after the fix
  • You can still drill into a single round via the Step 1 spans

Next: Step 6 — PII in logs.

docs.title: Step 6 — PII in logs
docs.text:
The labs/advanced/ directories keep their original feature-ordinal numbering, so they run one behind these doc steps — this page's assets live under labs/advanced/step5-pii-redaction/.

Goal: stop shipping player PII to Dynatrace. You will redact it at the collector first, then escalate to centrally managed redaction with BindPlane OP over the OTel Operator's OpAMP bridge when hand-rolled regex stops scaling. Budget 30 minutes.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
The casino logs player email, credit-card PAN, and SSN. Shipping that to Dynatrace is a compliance incident. Clean it at the collector (regex) first, then hand the config to BindPlane when per-service rules and audit requirements outgrow hand-maintained YAML.

flowchart LR casino["casino serviceslogs with email/PAN/SSN"] -->|OTLP logs| gw["gateway collector"] gw --> red["redaction + transform/piimask the PII"] red -->|clean logs| dt[("DynatraceLog Viewer")]

docs.title: Before — raw PII in the Log Viewer
docs.text:
The baseline gateway exports logs verbatim. A player-service line like:

charged player john.doe@example.com card 4111 1111 1111 1111 ssn 123-45-6789

lands in the Dynatrace Log Viewer with the PII intact.

docs.title: ② Opencode — redact at the collector
docs.text:
Drive opencode at the gateway with the otel-collector + otel-ottl skills — masking log PII is a transform, so name OTTL explicitly:

opencode run "Using the otel-collector and otel-ottl skills: in \
observability/collectors/gateway.yaml add redaction for player PII in LOG bodies — \
mask email, credit-card PAN, and SSN patterns (a transform/pii processor with \
OTTL replace_pattern on log.body, plus the redaction processor). Wire it into the \
logs pipeline only, after k8sattributes and before batch. Keep memory_limiter \
first and batch last."

docs.title: ③ Review — read the diff
docs.text:
Confirm the masking is on the logs pipeline, covers email/PAN/SSN, and sits between k8sattributes and batch. Reference answer: labs/advanced/step5-pii-redaction/redaction-processor.yaml.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

If it leaves one PII shape unmasked or masks trace attributes instead of log bodies, reply "mask all three — email, PAN, SSN — on log.body in the logs pipeline only." Always re-run the leak-scan DQL to confirm leaks == 0.

docs.title: ④ Apply — kubectl
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f observability/collectors/gateway.yaml

The same line now arrives as:

charged player ***EMAIL_REDACTED*** card ***PAN_REDACTED*** ssn ***SSN_REDACTED***

docs.title: Escalate — BindPlane OP via the OpAMP bridge (optional / stretch)
docs.text:
Optional / stretch

The collector redaction above already satisfies the Definition of done. This BindPlane escalation is a stretch exercise for cohorts with time — skip it to go straight to Step 7.

When regex-by-hand no longer scales (new PII shapes, per-service rules, audit trail), hand config to BindPlane OP over OpAMP. The OTel Operator's OpAMP bridge connects the operator-managed collectors to BindPlane, so redaction config is authored and pushed centrally instead of edited in YAML per collector.

flowchart LR BP["BindPlane OPMask Sensitive Data"] -- "OpAMP (ws)" --> BR["OpAMPBridgecasino-opamp-bridge"] BR -- "remote config" --> GW["otel-gateway-collector(operator-managed)"] GW -- "OTLP (clean)" --> DT[("Dynatrace")] 
# 1. BindPlane OP server in-cluster (pin the chart version for the training).
helm repo add bindplane https://observiq.github.io/bindplane-op-helm
helm upgrade --install bindplane bindplane/bindplane -n observability --create-namespace

# 2. Connection token for the bridge (BindPlane → Settings → OpAMP / install command).
kubectl -n observability create secret generic bindplane-opamp \
  --from-literal=BINDPLANE_OPAMP_TOKEN='<token-from-bindplane>'
kubectl -n observability set env opampbridge/casino-opamp-bridge --from=secret/bindplane-opamp

# 3. The OpAMP bridge.
kubectl apply -f labs/advanced/step5-pii-redaction/bindplane-opamp/opampbridge.yaml

In BindPlane, attach a Mask Sensitive Data processor to the casino log source and push — the bridge delivers it to otel-gateway-collector with no manual YAML.

Gotchas

  • The bridge image tag (operator-opamp-bridge:0.162.0) tracks the operator release line — keep it consistent with OTEL_OPERATOR_VERSION in observability/versions.env (currently v0.162.0; the bridge image omits the leading v).
  • componentsAllowed is an allow-list: BindPlane cannot push a component the bridge does not permit — a safety rail for the training cluster.
  • This supersedes the hand-rolled redaction/transform/pii once BindPlane owns the config; keep the Step 5 processors as the "before BindPlane" baseline.

docs.title: Dynatrace validation checkpoint
docs.text:
PII leak scan over the last hour — expect zero rows after the fix, in a Grail Notebook:

fetch logs, from: now() - 1h
| filter k8s.namespace.name == "casino"
| filter matchesValue(content, "*@*.*") or matchesValue(content, "*-**-****")
| summarize leaks = count()
  • Before: leaks > 0 — raw email/PAN/SSN visible in the Log Viewer.
  • After (redaction): leaks == 0; sampled lines show ***…_REDACTED***.
  • After (BindPlane): same clean result, now driven by the pushed BindPlane config; the OpAMPBridge reports healthy + effective-config in Dynatrace.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• Raw email/PAN/SSN confirmed in the Log Viewer before the fix
  • redaction + transform/pii wired into the logs pipeline
  • The leak-scan DQL returns leaks == 0
  • BindPlane OP + OpAMP bridge deployed; a Mask Sensitive Data config pushed
  • The OpAMPBridge reports healthy + effective-config

docs.title: Step 7 — Tail sampling
docs.text:
The labs/advanced/ directories keep their original feature-ordinal numbering, so they run one behind these doc steps — this page's assets live under labs/advanced/step6-tail-sampling/.

Goal: cut trace ingest cost sharply while keeping every trace that matters — errors, slow traces, and jackpots. Budget 25 minutes.

docs.title: The concept
docs.text:
Sampling is a strategy, not a failure — 100% is rarely the answer, but blind head sampling (deciding SDK-side, before the trace exists) throws away the errors you most need. Tail sampling buffers the whole trace, then keeps all errors / slow traces / jackpots and samples the boring majority down to 10%.

flowchart LR spans["all traces(buffered 10s)"] --> ts{"tail_samplingdecision"} ts -->|"status = ERROR"| keep1["keep 100%"] ts -->|"latency > 1s"| keep2["keep 100%"] ts -->|"casino.outcome = jackpot"| keep3["keep 100%"] ts -->|"everything else"| samp["keep 10%"] keep1 --> dt[("Dynatrace")] keep2 --> dt keep3 --> dt samp --> dt

docs.title: Before — export everything
docs.text: No sampling at the gateway — every trace is exported. Trace ingest cost scales linearly with casino load, and most of it is fast, successful, uninteresting spins.

docs.title: ② Opencode — tail sampling at the gateway
docs.text:
Drive opencode at the gateway with the otel-collector skill — goal (the four policies), target file, skill:

opencode run "Using the otel-collector skill: in observability/collectors/gateway.yaml \
add a tail_sampling processor to the TRACES pipeline with decision_wait 10s and \
four policies — status_code=ERROR keep 100%, latency>1s keep 100%, \
casino.outcome=jackpot keep 100%, and everything else probabilistic at 10%. Place \
it after k8sattributes/resource and before batch; keep memory_limiter first."

docs.title: ③ Review — read the diff
docs.text:
Confirm all four policies are present, decision_wait is 10s, and the processor is in the traces pipeline after k8sattributes/resource, before batch. Reference answer: labs/advanced/step6-tail-sampling/tail-sampling-processor.yaml.

If the agent gets it wrong — steer it back

If it drops the jackpot policy or samples errors, reply "errors, slow (>1s), and jackpots must each keep 100% — only the remaining 'boring' traces sample to 10%."

docs.title: ④ Apply — kubectl
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f observability/collectors/gateway.yaml

Policies: status_code=ERROR → 100%, latency > 1s → 100%, casino.outcome=jackpot → 100%, everything else → 10% probabilistic. The decision_wait buffer is 10s — long enough to assemble a full trace before deciding.

Single-instance requirement

Tail sampling must see all spans of a trace on one collector instance. The training gateway is replicas: 1, so this holds. If you scale the gateway out, you must front it with a loadbalancing exporter tier keyed on traceID — otherwise decisions are made on partial traces and you drop spans from traces you meant to keep.

docs.title: Dynatrace validation checkpoint
docs.text:
Confirm errors are retained while overall volume drops, in a Grail Notebook:

fetch spans, from: now() - 1h
| summarize kept = count() by { status = if(request.status == "failed", "error", "ok") }
  • Before: error traces are a small % of total, matching their natural rate; total volume is high.
  • After: total trace volume drops sharply, but the absolute count of error / slow / jackpot traces is unchanged (100% retention) — error analysis stays complete while cost falls. Verify a known error trace is still fully present end-to-end.

docs.title: Definition of done
docs.text:
• The tail_sampling processor is wired into the traces pipeline (after k8sattributes/resource, before batch)
  • The four policies are in place (error / slow / jackpot → 100%, else 10%)
  • Total trace volume drops after the fix
  • The absolute error/slow/jackpot count is unchanged
  • A known error trace is still complete end-to-end
